---
title: "Linear Regression from First Principles"
---

## Introduction {#sec-lr-intro}

Every method in this book that adjusts an indirect comparison for differences between trial
populations is, at its core, a regression. Simulated treatment comparison fits an outcome model on
individual patient data and then evaluates it at a comparator population; multilevel network
meta-regression writes the linear predictor of every arm as a regression on covariates; and
matching-adjusted indirect comparison reweights individuals to balance covariates, a procedure we will
see (Chapter 18) is closely tied to a weighted regression. Before any of that can be made rigorous we must
understand the simplest and most important regression model completely: the linear model, fit by
ordinary least squares. This chapter builds that theory from the ground up and proves every statement
it makes.

The questions we answer are the following. Given data, what does "the line of best fit" mean precisely,
and what formula produces it? In what sense is that formula optimal, and under what assumptions? If we
repeated the experiment, how would the estimate vary, and how do we quantify our uncertainty about it
with a confidence interval or a test? Finally, the philosophical question that justifies the whole
enterprise: why squares? Why minimize the sum of squared residuals rather than, say, the sum of absolute
residuals? We preview the answer at once, so the reader does not spend the chapter wondering: under
Gaussian errors, minimizing the sum of squares is exactly maximum likelihood (proved in @sec-lr-mle);
minimizing the sum of absolute residuals would instead be maximum likelihood under a different,
Laplace-shaped error model. The choice of squares is therefore a statement about the assumed shape of
the noise, not an arbitrary convention.

We will see that under the assumption of normal, homoskedastic (equal-variance), independent errors the
least-squares estimator is selected by four different optimality principles at once:

(i) **Projection (pure geometry).** The fitted vector is the point of the model space closest to the
data. This uses only linear algebra, no probability (@sec-lr-ols).

(ii) **Best linear unbiased estimator, BLUE (Gauss-Markov).** Among all estimators that are linear in
the data and unbiased, ordinary least squares has the smallest variance. This uses only the first two
moments of the errors, not their shape (@thm-ols-blue).

(iii) **Maximum likelihood estimator, MLE.** Under Gaussian errors, least squares is the coefficient
value that makes the observed data most probable (@thm-ols-mle-normal).

(iv) **Uniformly minimum-variance unbiased estimator, UMVU (Cramér-Rao).** Under Gaussian errors, no
unbiased estimator, linear or not, has smaller variance than least squares (@cor-ols-efficient-normal).

These are four genuinely different statements: (i) is geometric, (ii) ranges over linear estimators
assuming only two moments, (iii) is likelihood-based, and (iv) ranges over all unbiased estimators. That
they select the same estimator is the reason linear regression is the workhorse of applied statistics,
and it is the foundation on which the later chapters build.

**How to read this chapter.** Every result is proved in full, because every later chapter leans on these
facts and we want nothing downstream to be a black box. On a first reading you may take the formulas on
trust and skip the proofs without losing the through-line; the prose around each result tells you what it
means and why it matters for indirect comparison. The chapter is built in four layers, summarized here so
you always know which layer you are in.

| Layer | Where | What it delivers | Assumptions used |
|---|---|---|---|
| Geometry | @sec-lr-ols | the estimator, as a projection and as a formula | none (pure algebra) |
| Optimality without normality | @sec-lr-gm | OLS is BLUE; an unbiased variance estimate | G1, G2 |
| Exact inference | @sec-lr-normal, @sec-lr-inference | the $t$, $\chi^2$, and $F$ sampling distributions | G1, G2, G3 |
| When coefficients are not unique | @sec-lr-rank | estimability and the pseudoinverse | none (pure algebra) |

The development is self-contained but rests on the linear algebra of Chapters 1 to 3 (column spaces,
@thm-projection-theorem, the @thm-spectral-theorem) and the probability and inference of Chapters 4 and
5 (the multivariate normal, @def-mgf, @thm-cramer-rao). We recall what we use and prove everything that
is specific to regression.

## The linear model and its assumptions {#sec-lr-model}

Before the abstractions arrive, here is the concrete example we will return to at every transition.

::: {#exm-lr-running}
## A running example: a small two-arm trial
Six patients in a trial are randomized to a control arm or an active arm. For each patient we record the
change in HbA1c (a continuous glycemic outcome, where a more negative change is better) together with the
patient's baseline disease severity. To model the expected change we use three regressors: a constant
term, a treatment indicator $T$ (equal to $1$ on the active arm and $0$ on control), and the
mean-centered baseline severity $z$. In words,
$$
\mathbb{E}[\text{change}]=\beta_0\cdot 1+\beta_1\cdot T+\beta_2\cdot z .
$$
Each regressor is one column of the design matrix, and each carries a clinical role:

| Column of $\mathbf{X}$ | Meaning | Coefficient | Clinical role |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\mathbf{1}$ | constant (intercept) | $\beta_0$ | mean outcome in the reference arm at average covariates |
| $T$ | treatment indicator | $\beta_1$ | the adjusted treatment effect we care about |
| $z$ | baseline severity, centered | $\beta_2$ | a prognostic-covariate adjustment |
| ($\mathrm{age}$) | (a further covariate) | ($\beta_3$) | (a further adjustment, omitted below for hand arithmetic) |

Taking three patients per arm at centered baseline values $z=-1,0,1$, the design matrix and response are
$$
\mathbf{X}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&-1\\1&0&0\\1&0&1\\1&1&-1\\1&1&0\\1&1&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf{y}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\2\\-1\\0\\1\end{pmatrix},
$$
the first three rows being the control arm and the last three the active arm. We compute the fit in
@exm-lr-betahat and reuse this design when we reach the Gauss-Markov theorem and the variance formulas.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

We observe a response vector $\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^n$ and, for each of the $n$ units, the values of
$p$ regressors collected as the rows of a known matrix $\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$. The model
asserts that, up to random error, $\mathbf{y}$ lies in the column space $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$.

::: {#def-linear-model}
## The linear model
The **linear model** for a response $\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^n$ with design matrix
$\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$ ($p\le n$) is
$$
\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon},
$$ {#eq-linear-model}
where $\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\mathbb{R}^p$ is an unknown vector of coefficients and
$\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\in\mathbb{R}^n$ is an unobserved random error vector. The **Gauss-Markov
assumptions** are

(G1) **zero mean**, $\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}]=\mathbf{0}_n$;

(G2) **homoskedasticity and no correlation**, $\mathrm{Cov}(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon})=\sigma^2 I_n$ for
some unknown $\sigma^2>0$, that is, $\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon_i)=\sigma^2$ for every $i$ and
$\mathrm{Cov}(\varepsilon_i,\varepsilon_k)=0$ for $i\ne k$.

The model has **full column rank** when $\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X})=p$. For the exact distributional
theory of @sec-lr-normal onward we add

(G3) **normality**, $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}_n(\mathbf{0}_n,\sigma^2 I_n)$,

which (with G1, G2) is equivalent to $\mathbf{y}\sim\mathcal{N}_n(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^2
I_n)$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

**Reader translation.** The model says the response is a straight-line combination of the regressors,
$\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}$, plus random noise $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$ that on average is zero
(G1), has the same spread for every patient and does not link patients together (G2), and, when we want
exact tests, follows a bell curve (G3). In the running example $\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is the part
of a patient's HbA1c change explained by their arm and baseline severity, and
$\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$ is everything else.

A recurring source of confusion is the difference between the error and the residual. The table below
fixes the roles of the symbols used throughout the chapter.

| Symbol | Name | Observed? | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$ | error (disturbance) | no | the true random noise in @eq-linear-model; a property of nature |
| $\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ | residual | yes | what is left after fitting; computed from the data |
| $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ | coefficients | no | the true unknown effects |
| $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ | estimator | yes | our estimate of $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ from the data |
| $\sigma^2$ | error variance | no | the true noise variance in G2 |
| $s^2$ | variance estimate | yes | our estimate of $\sigma^2$ (@thm-sigma2-unbiased) |
| $\hat{\mathbf{y}}=\mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ | fitted values | yes | the model's prediction at each observed row |

The left-hand quantities $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon},\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^2$ are unknown features of
the population we never see; the right-hand quantities $\mathbf{r},\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}},s^2$ are
things we compute. Estimation is the act of guessing the first column from the second.

A few words on the content of the assumptions. Assumption G1 says the regressors capture the systematic
part of the response, so that the model $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{y}]=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is correct
on average; it forces $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{y}]\in\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$. Assumption G2 is two
assumptions in one: equal variances across units (homoskedasticity) and uncorrelated errors. It is what
makes ordinary, unweighted least squares the right procedure; when it fails one uses weighted or
generalized least squares, and the robust "sandwich" variance of @def-sandwich-variance repairs the
inference. Assumption G3 is needed only for exact, finite-sample tests and intervals; the point
estimator and the Gauss-Markov optimality of @sec-lr-gm require only G1 and G2.

::: {.remark}
**What homoskedasticity looks like, and when it fails.** Homoskedasticity (G2, first half) means every
patient's outcome scatters around the regression line by the same amount. Picture the data points: under
homoskedasticity they form a band of constant vertical thickness around the fitted line;
heteroskedasticity is a band that fans out, for example wider scatter at higher baseline severity. A
health researcher should expect G2 to fail when outcomes are recorded on different scales or in clusters:
sicker patients often vary more than healthy ones, and patients within the same hospital are correlated
(the second half of G2, no correlation, then also fails). When G2 fails, the point estimate
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ is still unbiased, but its reported standard errors are wrong. Two standard
repairs exist: weighted or generalized least squares (developed in @exr-lr-gm-weighted), which models the
unequal variances directly, and the robust "sandwich" variance estimator of @def-sandwich-variance, which
estimates the uncertainty of $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ without assuming the tidy $\sigma^2 I_n$
covariance structure at all. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reading the coefficients in health terms.** The coefficient $\beta_k$ is the conditional effect on
$\mathbb{E}[y_i]$ of a one-unit change in the $k$-th regressor with all others held fixed. The three
roles a column can play, which recur throughout the book, are visible already in the running example.

- The coefficient on the **treatment indicator**, $\beta_1$, is the adjusted treatment effect: the
  expected difference in outcome between the active and control arms for two patients with the same
  baseline severity. This is the quantity every indirect comparison ultimately targets.
- The coefficient on **baseline severity**, $\beta_2$, is a *prognostic* effect: severity predicts the
  outcome regardless of treatment. A covariate that influences the outcome but not the treatment effect
  is a prognostic variable (@def-prognostic-variable); you do not need the formal definition yet, only
  the picture of a covariate that shifts everyone's outcome.
- If we added a **treatment-by-severity product column**, its coefficient would measure how the treatment
  effect itself changes with severity. A covariate that changes the treatment effect is an *effect
  modifier* (@def-effect-modifier). Effect modifiers are the central obstacle in indirect comparison: two
  trials with different severity mixes can report different treatment effects even when nothing else
  differs. We meet them properly in Part II.

On the identity link used here, this conditional reading is also the marginal (population-averaged) one,
so the distinctions stay simple. For the nonlinear links of Chapter 7 the conditional and marginal
effects diverge, a phenomenon named @def-non-collapsibility. The clean behavior of the identity-link
linear model is exactly why it is the right place to learn the machinery before meeting its
complications. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

Throughout @sec-lr-ols to @sec-lr-anova we assume **full column rank**, $\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X})=p$.
In plain terms this means no regressor column can be reconstructed as a combination of the others, so
each coefficient is separately identifiable: the data can tell the columns apart. The assumption fails in
familiar situations, for example when a categorical predictor is coded with an intercept *and* a separate
indicator for every level, so that the indicators add up to the intercept column. We treat that
rank-deficient case fully in @sec-lr-rank, where the geometry survives intact and only the coordinate
vector $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ becomes non-unique; a reader who meets a coding problem of this kind in
practice can jump ahead to that section without loss. The following small lemma is the algebraic hinge of
the full-rank theory: it is what makes $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}$ invertible.

::: {#lem-gram-nullspace}
## Null space of the Gram matrix
For any $\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$,
$\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X})$ and
$\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})=\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}^\top)$; consequently
$\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})=\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X})$. In particular
$\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}$ is invertible if and only if $\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X})=p$, in which case it
is positive definite.
:::

::: {.proof}
We argue in four short steps.

*Step 1 (the two null spaces are equal).* If $\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ then
$\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$, so
$\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X})\subseteq\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})$. Conversely, if
$\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ then
$$
0=\mathbf{v}^\top\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v}=(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v})^\top(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v})
=\|\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v}\|_2^2,
$$
whence $\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ (a vector of norm zero is the zero vector); thus
$\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})\subseteq\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X})$ and the two null spaces are
equal.

*Step 2 (the ranks are equal).* Apply the rank-nullity theorem (@thm-rank-nullity) to the $p\times p$
matrix $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}$ and to $\mathbf{X}$, both of which have $p$ columns. Rank-nullity says
(number of columns) $=$ rank $+$ nullity, so
$$
\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})=p-\dim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})
=p-\dim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X})=\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X}),
$$
the middle equality being Step 1.

*Step 3 (the column spaces are equal).* The inclusion
$\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})\subseteq\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}^\top)$ is immediate, because every
column of $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{X}^\top(\mathbf{X})$ is $\mathbf{X}^\top$ times a column of
$\mathbf{X}$. To upgrade this inclusion to equality it suffices to show the two spaces have the same
dimension. The dimension of $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})$ is $\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X}^\top
\mathbf{X})=\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X})$ by Step 2, while the dimension of $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}^\top)$ is
$\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X}^\top)$, and a basic fact of linear algebra is that a matrix and its transpose
have the same rank, $\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X}^\top)=\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X})$ (this is part of the
fundamental theorem of the four subspaces, @thm-four-subspaces; row rank equals column rank). The two
dimensions match, so the inclusion is an equality.

*Step 4 (definiteness and invertibility).* The matrix $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}$ is symmetric with
$\mathbf{v}^\top\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v}=\|\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v}\|_2^2\ge 0$, so it is positive
semidefinite. It is positive definite exactly when $\|\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v}\|_2^2>0$ for every
$\mathbf{v}\ne\mathbf{0}$, that is, when $\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X})=\{\mathbf{0}\}$, equivalently
$\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X})=p$ (@thm-pd-characterization). A positive definite matrix is invertible. $\square$
:::

**Reader translation.** The Gram matrix $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}$ inherits exactly the
non-redundancy of $\mathbf{X}$: it is invertible if and only if the regressors are not redundant. This is
the single fact that lets us write down the closed-form estimator @eq-betahat below; when it fails we are
in the rank-deficient world of @sec-lr-rank.

## Ordinary least squares: two derivations {#sec-lr-ols}

We measure the fit of a candidate coefficient vector $\mathbf{b}$ by the sum of squared residuals.

::: {#def-sums-of-squares}
## Residual, total, and explained sums of squares
For a candidate $\mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{R}^p$ the **objective function** is
$$
S(\mathbf{b}) = \|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\mathbf{b}\|_2^2
= (\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\mathbf{b})^\top(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\mathbf{b}).
$$
At a minimizer $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ write the fitted values $\hat{\mathbf{y}}=\mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$
and residuals $\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}}$. The **residual sum of squares** is
$\mathrm{RSS}=\|\mathbf{r}\|_2^2=S(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})$. When the model contains an intercept
(the vector $\mathbf{1}_n$ lies in $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$) the **total sum of squares** is
$\mathrm{TSS}=\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\bar y)^2=\|\mathbf{y}-\bar y\,\mathbf{1}_n\|_2^2$ with $\bar
y=\tfrac1n\sum_i y_i$, and the **explained sum of squares** is
$\mathrm{ESS}_{\mathrm{reg}}=\|\hat{\mathbf{y}}-\bar y\,\mathbf{1}_n\|_2^2$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

**Reader translation.** $S(\mathbf{b})$ is the total squared miss if we used the coefficients
$\mathbf{b}$; least squares picks the $\mathbf{b}$ that makes it smallest. Once we have the winner
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$, the RSS is the leftover squared error, the TSS is the total spread of the
response around its mean, and the explained sum of squares is the part of that spread the regression
accounts for.

::: {.remark}
**A notation trap.** The subscript on $\mathrm{ESS}_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is deliberate. Later chapters use the
bare symbol $\mathrm{ESS}$ for the *effective sample size* of a weighted sample (central to MAIC in
Chapter 18), an entirely different quantity. We always write the subscript here, $\mathrm{ESS}_{\mathrm{reg}}$,
for the explained regression sum of squares, to keep the two apart. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

### Derivation by calculus

::: {#thm-ols-normal-equations}
## Normal equations and the least-squares estimator
A vector $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathbb{R}^p$ minimizes $S$ over $\mathbb{R}^p$ if and only if it
solves the **normal equations**
$$
\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\,\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}.
$$ {#eq-normal-equations}
The normal equations are always consistent. When $\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X})=p$ the minimizer is unique
and equals
$$
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}.
$$ {#eq-betahat}
:::

::: {.proof}
Expand the objective, using $\mathbf{b}^\top\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{y}^\top\mathbf{X}\mathbf{b}$
(a scalar equals its transpose):
$$
S(\mathbf{b})=\mathbf{y}^\top\mathbf{y}-2\,\mathbf{b}^\top\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}
+\mathbf{b}^\top\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\,\mathbf{b}.
$$
This is a quadratic form in $\mathbf{b}$ (a function built from the squared shape
$\mathbf{b}^\top A\mathbf{b}$ for a symmetric matrix $A=\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}$; see
@def-quadratic-form), with gradient and Hessian
$$
\nabla S(\mathbf{b})=-2\,\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}+2\,\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\,\mathbf{b},
\qquad
\nabla^2 S(\mathbf{b})=2\,\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}.
$$
The gradient is the multivariable analogue of the single-variable derivative: setting it to zero is the
same first-order condition as in one-variable calculus, $\tfrac{d}{db}\sum_i(y_i-b\,x_i)^2=0$, written
once for all $p$ coordinates at once. By @lem-gram-nullspace the Hessian $2\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}$ is
positive semidefinite everywhere, so
$S$ is a convex function on $\mathbb{R}^p$; for a differentiable convex function a point is a global
minimizer if and only if its gradient vanishes there (a fact we now verify directly so as not to lean on
convex-analysis machinery). Setting $\nabla S(\mathbf{b})=\mathbf{0}$ gives exactly the normal equations
@eq-normal-equations. We prove the two directions of the "if and only if" separately.

*Forward direction (a solution of the normal equations is a global minimizer).* Let
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ solve @eq-normal-equations and let $\mathbf{b}=\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+\mathbf{d}$
be arbitrary. Then
$$
S(\mathbf{b})-S(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})
=-2\,\mathbf{d}^\top\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}
+2\,\mathbf{d}^\top\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
+\mathbf{d}^\top\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\mathbf{d}
=2\,\mathbf{d}^\top\!\big(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}\big)
+\|\mathbf{X}\mathbf{d}\|_2^2
=\|\mathbf{X}\mathbf{d}\|_2^2\ge 0,
$$
the linear term vanishing because $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ solves @eq-normal-equations. Hence
$S(\mathbf{b})\ge S(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})$ for every $\mathbf{b}$, so every solution of the normal
equations is a global minimizer.

*Reverse direction (a minimizer solves the normal equations).* Conversely, if $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$
is a minimizer then $\nabla S(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\mathbf{0}$ (a necessary first-order condition for
an interior minimum of a differentiable function on $\mathbb{R}^p$), which is @eq-normal-equations.

Consistency holds because $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}\in\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}^\top)
=\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})$ by @lem-gram-nullspace, so the right-hand side lies in the
column space of the coefficient matrix. In plain terms: the normal equations always have at least one
solution; they may simply fail to have a *unique* one when the design is rank deficient (the case of
@sec-lr-rank). When $\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X})=p$, @lem-gram-nullspace makes
$\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}$ invertible, so @eq-normal-equations has the unique solution
@eq-betahat. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why "normal"?** Here "normal" is the geometric word for *perpendicular*. The equations
$\mathbf{X}^\top(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\mathbf{0}$ say the residual is
perpendicular to every column of $\mathbf{X}$. The projection derivation below makes this geometry
explicit. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

We make the formula concrete at once, rather than waiting for the end of the chapter.

::: {#exm-lr-betahat}
## The running example: computing the estimate
For the trial design of @exm-lr-running, the Gram matrix is block structured because the centered
baseline $z$ is balanced across arms (its column is orthogonal to both the intercept and the treatment
column):
$$
\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}=\begin{pmatrix}6&3&0\\3&3&0\\0&0&4\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}\tfrac13&-\tfrac13&0\\[2pt]-\tfrac13&\tfrac23&0\\[2pt]0&0&\tfrac14\end{pmatrix}.
$$
With $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}=(3,0,4)^\top$ (the column sums of $\mathbf{y}$, of $T y$, and of $z y$),
$$
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}
=\begin{pmatrix}\tfrac13(3)-\tfrac13(0)\\[2pt]-\tfrac13(3)+\tfrac23(0)\\[2pt]\tfrac14(4)\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}.
$$
Reading the three numbers clinically: the control arm's expected HbA1c change at average baseline is
$\hat\beta_0=1$; the **adjusted treatment effect** is $\hat\beta_1=-1$, so the active arm lowers the
change by one unit (an improvement); and each one-unit rise in baseline severity adds
$\hat\beta_2=1$ to the expected change. These illustrative values happen to fit exactly, so every residual
is zero here; the worked example of @sec-lr-example carries a data set with genuine scatter through every
variance and testing formula. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

**Why this matters (ITC).** This predict-from-coefficients step is the engine of simulated treatment
comparison (Chapter 19). There one fits exactly this kind of outcome model on individual patient data
from one trial, then evaluates $\mathbf{x}^\top\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ at the *comparator* trial's mean
covariates to predict how the treatment would have performed in the other population. The normal
equations are precisely what make that prediction well-defined.

### Derivation by projection

The calculus derivation produces the formula but hides its meaning. The projection derivation reveals
that least squares is geometry: $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is the point of $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$ closest to
$\mathbf{y}$.

::: {.proof}
**(Projection derivation of @thm-ols-normal-equations.)** Minimizing
$S(\mathbf{b})=\|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\mathbf{b}\|_2^2$ over $\mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{R}^p$ is the same as
minimizing $\|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{v}\|_2^2$ over $\mathbf{v}\in\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$, because as
$\mathbf{b}$ ranges over $\mathbb{R}^p$ the vector $\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{X}\mathbf{b}$ ranges over exactly
$\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$ (@def-column-space). The orthogonal projection theorem
(@thm-projection-theorem) states that the closed subspace $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$ contains a unique
closest point $\hat{\mathbf{y}}=P_{\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})}\mathbf{y}$ to $\mathbf{y}$, characterized by
the orthogonality of the residual to the subspace:
$\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}}\perp\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$. Orthogonality to $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$
means orthogonality to each column of $\mathbf{X}$, that is,
$\mathbf{X}^\top(\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}})=\mathbf{0}$. Writing
$\hat{\mathbf{y}}=\mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ this is
$\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$, the normal equations
@eq-normal-equations once more. When $\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X})=p$ the representation
$\hat{\mathbf{y}}=\mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ is unique and @eq-betahat follows. $\square$
:::

The picture behind the projection derivation is the single most useful image in the chapter. The data
$\mathbf{y}$ is a point in $\mathbb{R}^n$; the model space $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$ is a flat subspace
(a line, a plane, or higher); and the fitted vector $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is the foot of the perpendicular
dropped from $\mathbf{y}$ onto that subspace, with the residual $\mathbf{r}$ as the perpendicular itself.

```
        y      (the data: a point in R^n)
        |\
        | \    r = y - yhat   (residual: perpendicular to the model space)
        |  \
        |   \
   -----+----*--------------------------  C(X): the model space {Xb : b in R^p}
             yhat = Hy
             (fitted values: the closest point of C(X) to y; right angle at yhat)
```

**Reader translation.** "Line of best fit" is made exact: among all predictions the model can produce
(every point of $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$), the fitted values are the unique one nearest the data, and
"nearest" forces the leftover error to be perpendicular to the model. Everything else in the chapter is
a consequence of this right angle.

::: {.remark}
The two derivations are the same computation read in two directions. The vanishing gradient
$\mathbf{X}^\top(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\mathbf{b})=\mathbf{0}$ *is* the statement that the residual is
orthogonal to every column of $\mathbf{X}$. Calculus supplies the formula and convexity certifies it is
a global minimum; projection supplies the picture and explains why the minimum is unique on the level of
fitted values even when it is not unique on the level of coefficients (the theme of @sec-lr-rank).
Numerically one rarely forms $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}$ and inverts it; the orthogonal factorization
$\mathbf{X}=QR$ from Gram-Schmidt (@thm-gram-schmidt) gives the more stable solution of
$R\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=Q^\top\mathbf{y}$. This is what statistical software actually does: the `lm()`
routine in R, and its equivalents, never form $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}$ explicitly but factor
$\mathbf{X}$ directly, which is numerically more accurate. The closed form @eq-betahat is for
understanding and proof, not for computation. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

### The hat matrix and the residual maker

::: {#def-hat-matrix}
## Hat matrix and residual maker
Under $\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X})=p$ the **hat matrix** is
$$
H=\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n},
$$ {#eq-hat-matrix}
so that the fitted values are $\hat{\mathbf{y}}=H\mathbf{y}$ (it "puts the hat on $\mathbf{y}$"). The
**residual maker** is $M=I_n-H$, so that the residuals are $\mathbf{r}=M\mathbf{y}$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

**Reader translation.** $H$ is the single matrix that turns data into fitted values, $\hat{\mathbf{y}}=H
\mathbf{y}$, and $M=I_n-H$ turns data into residuals, $\mathbf{r}=M\mathbf{y}$. They do all the work of
fitting in one multiplication each.

::: {.remark}
**Why you should care about $H$: diagnostics.** The hat matrix is not a mere bookkeeping device. Its
$i$-th diagonal entry $h_{ii}$, called the **leverage** of observation $i$, measures how strongly that
observation pulls its own fitted value toward itself; a high-leverage patient (one with unusual covariate
values) can dominate the fit. Leverage is the basis of every regression diagnostic an applied researcher
meets, including Cook's distance for influential points. We develop the formal properties of leverage in
@exr-lr-leverage. The idempotence $H^2=H$ proved next also has a plain meaning: fitting is a projection,
so once you have projected onto the model space, projecting again changes nothing. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#lem-hat-properties}
## Properties of H and M
With $H$ and $M$ as in @def-hat-matrix:

1. $H$ and $M$ are symmetric and idempotent: $H^\top=H$, $H^2=H$, $M^\top=M$, $M^2=M$.
2. $HM=MH=0$.
3. $H\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{X}$ and $M\mathbf{X}=0$; equivalently $\mathbf{X}^\top H=\mathbf{X}^\top$ and
   $\mathbf{X}^\top M=0$.
4. $H$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$ and $M$ the orthogonal projection
   onto $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})^\perp=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X}^\top)$.
5. $\mathrm{tr}(H)=p$ and $\mathrm{tr}(M)=n-p$.
:::

::: {.proof}
(1) Symmetry of $H$: since $(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}$ is symmetric (the inverse of a symmetric
matrix is symmetric),
$H^\top=\mathbf{X}\big((\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\big)^\top\mathbf{X}^\top
=\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top=H$. Idempotence:
$$
H^2=\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\underbrace{\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}}_{=I_p}\mathbf{X}^\top
=\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top=H.
$$
Then $M^\top=(I-H)^\top=I-H=M$ and $M^2=(I-H)^2=I-2H+H^2=I-2H+H=I-H=M$.

(2) $HM=H(I-H)=H-H^2=H-H=0$, and $MH=(I-H)H=H-H^2=0$.

(3) $H\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{X}I_p=\mathbf{X}$,
hence $M\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{X}-H\mathbf{X}=0$. Transposing and using symmetry gives
$\mathbf{X}^\top H=\mathbf{X}^\top$ and $\mathbf{X}^\top M=0$.

(4) A symmetric idempotent matrix is the orthogonal projection onto its column space
(@thm-projection-matrix-characterization). By (3), $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})\subseteq\mathcal{C}(H)$; conversely every
column of $H$ is $\mathbf{X}$ times a vector, so $\mathcal{C}(H)\subseteq\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$; thus
$\mathcal{C}(H)=\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$ and $H=P_{\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})}$. Then
$M=I_n-H=P^{\perp}_{\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})}$ is the orthogonal projection onto
$\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})^\perp$ (@lem-projection-linear). The identity
$\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})^\perp=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X}^\top)$ is the fundamental theorem of the four
subspaces (@thm-four-subspaces).

(5) Using the cyclic property of the trace,
$\mathrm{tr}(H)=\mathrm{tr}\big(\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\big)
=\mathrm{tr}\big((\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\big)=\mathrm{tr}(I_p)=p$,
and $\mathrm{tr}(M)=\mathrm{tr}(I_n)-\mathrm{tr}(H)=n-p$. $\square$
:::

**Why this matters.** These five properties are the algebraic toolkit reused in almost every proof that
follows: idempotence and symmetry drive the distribution of the residual sum of squares (@thm-rss-chisq),
$HM=0$ drives the independence of the estimate and the variance estimate (@thm-betahat-s2-independence),
and $\mathrm{tr}(M)=n-p$ is the source of the degrees-of-freedom divisor.

::: {#prp-fitted-residual-geometry}
## Geometry of fitted values and residuals
The fitted values and residuals satisfy $\hat{\mathbf{y}}\in\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$,
$\mathbf{r}\in\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})^\perp$, and $\hat{\mathbf{y}}^\top\mathbf{r}=0$. Consequently
$\mathbf{y}=\hat{\mathbf{y}}+\mathbf{r}$ is the orthogonal decomposition of $\mathbf{y}$ into its
component in the model space and its component orthogonal to it, and
$$
\|\mathbf{y}\|_2^2=\|\hat{\mathbf{y}}\|_2^2+\|\mathbf{r}\|_2^2 .
$$
If the model contains an intercept then in addition $\sum_{i=1}^n r_i=0$, so the residuals have mean
zero and $\overline{\hat y}=\bar y$.
:::

::: {.proof}
$\hat{\mathbf{y}}=H\mathbf{y}\in\mathcal{C}(H)=\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$ and $\mathbf{r}=M\mathbf{y}\in
\mathcal{C}(M)=\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})^\perp$ by parts (3) and (4) of @lem-hat-properties. Their inner
product is $\hat{\mathbf{y}}^\top\mathbf{r}=(H\mathbf{y})^\top(M\mathbf{y})
=\mathbf{y}^\top H M\mathbf{y}=0$ by part (2). Since $\hat{\mathbf{y}}\perp\mathbf{r}$, the Pythagorean
theorem gives
$\|\mathbf{y}\|_2^2=\|\hat{\mathbf{y}}+\mathbf{r}\|_2^2=\|\hat{\mathbf{y}}\|_2^2+\|\mathbf{r}\|_2^2$.
If $\mathbf{1}_n\in\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$ then $H\mathbf{1}_n=\mathbf{1}_n$, so $M\mathbf{1}_n=\mathbf{0}$
and $\sum_i r_i=\mathbf{1}_n^\top\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{1}_n^\top M\mathbf{y}=(M\mathbf{1}_n)^\top\mathbf{y}=0$.
Then $\overline{\hat y}=\bar y-\tfrac1n\sum_i r_i=\bar y$. $\square$
:::

**Reader translation.** The data splits cleanly into "what the model captured" ($\hat{\mathbf{y}}$) and
"what it missed" ($\mathbf{r}$), and these two parts are at right angles, so their squared lengths add
(Pythagoras). When the model has an intercept the residuals also sum to zero, which is why the fitted
line passes through the average point $(\bar x,\bar y)$. This orthogonal split is what the
analysis-of-variance decomposition (@sec-lr-anova) and $R^2$ will measure.

## The Gauss-Markov theorem {#sec-lr-gm}

We now bring in the assumptions G1 and G2 and study $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ as a random vector. We use
repeatedly the two rules of linear transformation of moments: for a fixed matrix $A$ and random vector
$\mathbf{z}$, $\mathbb{E}[A\mathbf{z}]=A\,\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{z}]$ and
$\mathrm{Cov}(A\mathbf{z})=A\,\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{z})\,A^\top$. The second follows from the definition:
$\mathrm{Cov}(A\mathbf{z})=\mathbb{E}\big[A(\mathbf{z}-\mathbb{E}\mathbf{z})(\mathbf{z}-\mathbb{E}\mathbf{z})^\top
A^\top\big]=A\,\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{z})\,A^\top$.

::: {#thm-ols-moments}
## Mean and covariance of the OLS estimator
Under @def-linear-model with G1, G2 and $\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X})=p$, the estimator @eq-betahat is
unbiased and has covariance
$$
\mathbb{E}[\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]=\boldsymbol{\beta},
\qquad
\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}.
$$ {#eq-cov-betahat}
:::

::: {.proof}
Substitute @eq-linear-model into @eq-betahat and set $A=(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top$:
$$
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=A(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\varepsilon})
=(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\,\boldsymbol{\beta}
+A\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}
=\boldsymbol{\beta}+A\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}.
$$ {#eq-betahat-error}
Taking expectations and using G1, $\mathbb{E}[\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]
=\boldsymbol{\beta}+A\,\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}]=\boldsymbol{\beta}$. For the covariance,
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta}=A\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$, so by G2,
$$
\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=A\,\mathrm{Cov}(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon})\,A^\top
=A(\sigma^2 I_n)A^\top
=\sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}
=\sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1},
$$
where we used the symmetry of $(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}$. $\square$
:::

**Reader translation.** On average the estimator hits the true coefficients (unbiased), and its
uncertainty is governed entirely by $\sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}$, which depends on the
design but not on the data values $\mathbf{y}$. In the running example
(@exm-lr-betahat), the $(T,T)$ entry of $(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}$ is $\tfrac23$, so the variance
of the estimated treatment effect is $\sigma^2\cdot\tfrac23$ and its standard error is $\sigma\sqrt{2/3}$.
A design that estimates the treatment effect more precisely is one that makes this diagonal entry small.

Among unbiased estimators that are linear in $\mathbf{y}$, none has a smaller variance than OLS. This is
the Gauss-Markov theorem, the central optimality result of the chapter. "Best" is meant in the strong
matrix sense made precise next.

::: {#def-loewner-order}
## Loewner order
For symmetric matrices $A$ and $B$ of the same size, write $A\succeq B$, and say $A$ dominates $B$ in the
**Loewner order**, when the difference $A-B$ is positive semidefinite, that is $\mathbf{z}^\top(A-B)
\mathbf{z}\ge 0$ for every vector $\mathbf{z}$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

**Reader translation.** When $A$ and $B$ are the covariance matrices of two estimators, $A\succeq B$ is a
strong statement. Taking $\mathbf{z}=\mathbf{c}$ it gives $\mathbf{c}^\top A\mathbf{c}\ge\mathbf{c}^\top B
\mathbf{c}$, that is, *every* linear combination $\mathbf{c}^\top\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ of the
coefficients has at least as large a variance under $A$ as under $B$. A single matrix inequality
therefore compares the two estimators on every question at once, not one coefficient at a time.

::: {#thm-ols-blue}
## Gauss-Markov
Assume @def-linear-model with G1, G2 and $\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X})=p$. Let
$\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=C\mathbf{y}$ be any estimator linear in $\mathbf{y}$ that is unbiased for
$\boldsymbol{\beta}$ for every value of $\boldsymbol{\beta}$. Then
$$
\mathrm{Cov}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}})-\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\succeq 0,
$$
with equality if and only if $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ almost surely.
In particular, for every fixed $\mathbf{c}\in\mathbb{R}^p$ the OLS estimator $\mathbf{c}^\top
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ has the smallest variance among all linear unbiased estimators of
$\mathbf{c}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}$: $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ is the **best linear unbiased estimator**
(BLUE).
:::

**Roadmap of the proof.** Write any rival linear unbiased estimator as $C\mathbf{y}$. Unbiasedness forces
$C\mathbf{X}=I_p$. We split $C=A+D$ into the OLS map $A=(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top$
plus a remainder $D$; read $D$ as whatever extra linear operation the rival performs on top of OLS.
Unbiasedness forces that extra operation to ignore the model space, $D\mathbf{X}=0$, and this single fact
makes the cross terms vanish, leaving the rival's covariance equal to the OLS covariance plus a
nonnegative piece $\sigma^2 DD^\top$. Hence the rival can never beat OLS, and ties it only when $D=0$.

::: {.proof}
Unbiasedness of $C\mathbf{y}$ for all $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ means
$\mathbb{E}[C\mathbf{y}]=C\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\boldsymbol{\beta}$ for every
$\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\mathbb{R}^p$, which forces
$$
C\mathbf{X}=I_p.
$$
Write $C=A+D$ with $A=(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top$ the OLS map, so $D=C-A$. From
$C\mathbf{X}=I_p$ and $A\mathbf{X}=(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}=I_p$ we get
$$
D\mathbf{X}=C\mathbf{X}-A\mathbf{X}=I_p-I_p=0 .
$$
Now compute the covariance of $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=C\mathbf{y}$ using $\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{y})
=\sigma^2 I_n$:
$$
\mathrm{Cov}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\sigma^2 C C^\top=\sigma^2 (A+D)(A+D)^\top
=\sigma^2\big(AA^\top+AD^\top+DA^\top+DD^\top\big).
$$
The cross terms vanish: $AD^\top=(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top D^\top
=(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}(D\mathbf{X})^\top=0$, and $DA^\top=(AD^\top)^\top=0$. Since
$AA^\top=(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}=\sigma^{-2}\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})$, we obtain
$$
\mathrm{Cov}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}})
=\sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}+\sigma^2 DD^\top
=\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})+\sigma^2 DD^\top .
$$ {#eq-gm-decomp}
For any $\mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{R}^p$, $\mathbf{z}^\top DD^\top\mathbf{z}=\|D^\top\mathbf{z}\|_2^2\ge 0$,
so $DD^\top\succeq 0$ and the difference of covariance matrices is positive semidefinite. Taking
$\mathbf{z}=\mathbf{c}$ gives the scalar conclusion
$\mathrm{Var}(\mathbf{c}^\top\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}})
=\mathrm{Var}(\mathbf{c}^\top\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})+\sigma^2\|D^\top\mathbf{c}\|_2^2
\ge\mathrm{Var}(\mathbf{c}^\top\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})$.

Equality in the Loewner order means $\mathbf{z}^\top DD^\top\mathbf{z}=\|D^\top\mathbf{z}\|_2^2=0$ for
all $\mathbf{z}$, hence $D^\top=0$, hence $D=0$ and $C=A$, so
$\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=A\mathbf{y}=\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$. $\square$
:::

**Why this matters (ITC).** In plain terms, when you fit `lm(y ~ x)` and read off the standard errors,
Gauss-Markov says you are getting the best you can do among linear unbiased estimators using only the
two assumptions G1 and G2, with no appeal to normality. A caution for later: weighted least squares is
optimal only when the weights invert the error covariance (@exr-lr-gm-weighted). Matching-adjusted
indirect comparison (Chapter 18) also weights patients, but its weights balance covariates against a
target population; they change the estimand and cost precision, so Gauss-Markov optimality does not
transfer to it.

::: {.remark}
The proof uses only G1 and G2. Normality (G3) is not needed for Gauss-Markov optimality. The price of
the restriction to *linear* estimators is real: under non-normal errors there can be nonlinear unbiased
estimators that beat OLS. Under normality, however, no such estimator exists, even nonlinear ones; we
prove this stronger statement in @cor-ols-efficient-normal. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

To use @eq-cov-betahat in practice we must estimate the unknown $\sigma^2$. The natural estimator
divides the residual sum of squares not by $n$ but by $n-p$, the dimension of the residual space; this
exact divisor makes the estimator unbiased.

::: {.remark}
**The trace trick.** Two facts from Chapter 1 are used repeatedly below. First, a $1\times 1$ matrix
equals its own trace, so any scalar can be written $a=\mathrm{tr}(a)$. Second, the trace is linear and
*cyclic*: $\mathrm{tr}(BC)=\mathrm{tr}(CB)$ whenever both products are defined. Together they let us pull
a random vector out of a quadratic form and replace the expectation by a covariance matrix, which is the
key maneuver in the next proof and again in @thm-rss-chisq. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#thm-sigma2-unbiased}
## Unbiased estimation of the error variance
Under @def-linear-model with G1, G2 and $\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X})=p$ (and $n>p$), the statistic
$$
s^2=\frac{\mathrm{RSS}}{n-p}=\frac{\|\mathbf{r}\|_2^2}{n-p}=\frac{\mathbf{y}^\top M\mathbf{y}}{n-p}
$$
is unbiased for $\sigma^2$: $\mathbb{E}[s^2]=\sigma^2$.
:::

::: {.proof}
First, $\mathrm{RSS}=\mathbf{r}^\top\mathbf{r}=(M\mathbf{y})^\top(M\mathbf{y})
=\mathbf{y}^\top M^\top M\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{y}^\top M\mathbf{y}$ by the symmetry and idempotence of $M$
(@lem-hat-properties). Substitute $\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$ and
use $M\mathbf{X}=0$:
$$
\mathbf{y}^\top M\mathbf{y}
=(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\varepsilon})^\top M(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\varepsilon})
=\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^\top M\boldsymbol{\varepsilon},
$$
the terms involving $\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}$ vanishing because
$M\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}=\mathbf{0}$ and
$(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})^\top M=(M\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})^\top=\mathbf{0}^\top$. Now take the
expectation of the scalar $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^\top M\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$ using the trace
trick: a scalar equals its own trace, and the trace is linear and cyclic, so
$$
\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^\top M\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}]
=\mathbb{E}\big[\mathrm{tr}(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^\top M\boldsymbol{\varepsilon})\big]
=\mathbb{E}\big[\mathrm{tr}(M\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^\top)\big]
=\mathrm{tr}\big(M\,\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^\top]\big)
=\mathrm{tr}(M\,\sigma^2 I_n)=\sigma^2\,\mathrm{tr}(M)=\sigma^2(n-p),
$$
using $\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^\top]
=\mathrm{Cov}(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon})=\sigma^2 I_n$ from G1, G2 and $\mathrm{tr}(M)=n-p$ from
@lem-hat-properties. Dividing by $n-p$ gives $\mathbb{E}[s^2]=\sigma^2$. $\square$
:::

**Why this matters.** $s^2$ is the number reported as the residual variance (its square root, the
residual standard error, appears in every regression printout), and it feeds every standard error and
every $t$ and $F$ statistic later in the chapter. Getting its expectation exactly right, via the divisor
$n-p$ rather than $n$, is what makes those downstream tests unbiased.

::: {.remark}
The divisor $n-p$ has a clean geometric reading: the residual lives in the $(n-p)$-dimensional space
$\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})^\perp$, so although there are $n$ residuals they satisfy $p$ linear constraints
(the normal equations), leaving $n-p$ free coordinates. Each contributes one "degree of freedom" of
variance. We make this exact in @thm-rss-chisq. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Normal-theory distribution results {#sec-lr-normal}

To build confidence intervals and tests we need the full sampling distribution of
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ and $s^2$, not only their first two moments. Here we invoke G3. We first
record two facts about the multivariate normal that we use repeatedly; both are proved with the moment
generating function (@def-mgf), whose value for $\mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{N}_n(\boldsymbol{\mu},\Sigma)$ is
$M_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{t})=\exp\!\big(\mathbf{t}^\top\boldsymbol{\mu}+\tfrac12\mathbf{t}^\top\Sigma
\mathbf{t}\big)$, and which determines the distribution uniquely (both facts are established in
Chapter 4).

Treat the moment generating function as a fingerprint of a distribution. Two facts from Chapter 4 are all
we need, and we do not reprove them. First, the fingerprint determines the distribution: if a random
vector's moment generating function matches that of a known normal, then it *is* that normal. Second, the
joint fingerprint factors into a product of separate fingerprints exactly when the pieces are
independent. These are the only two properties of the moment generating function we exploit below.

### Two facts about the multivariate normal we will reuse

::: {#lem-mvn-affine-closure}
## Affine closure of the multivariate normal
If $\mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{N}_n(\boldsymbol{\mu},\Sigma)$, $A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ and
$\mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{R}^m$, then
$A\mathbf{z}+\mathbf{b}\sim\mathcal{N}_m(A\boldsymbol{\mu}+\mathbf{b},A\Sigma A^\top)$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Let $\mathbf{w}=A\mathbf{z}+\mathbf{b}$. For $\mathbf{s}\in\mathbb{R}^m$,
$$
M_{\mathbf{w}}(\mathbf{s})=\mathbb{E}\big[e^{\mathbf{s}^\top(A\mathbf{z}+\mathbf{b})}\big]
=e^{\mathbf{s}^\top\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbb{E}\big[e^{(A^\top\mathbf{s})^\top\mathbf{z}}\big]
=e^{\mathbf{s}^\top\mathbf{b}}\,M_{\mathbf{z}}(A^\top\mathbf{s})
=e^{\mathbf{s}^\top\mathbf{b}}\exp\!\Big((A^\top\mathbf{s})^\top\boldsymbol{\mu}
+\tfrac12(A^\top\mathbf{s})^\top\Sigma(A^\top\mathbf{s})\Big).
$$
Collecting terms, the exponent equals $\mathbf{s}^\top(A\boldsymbol{\mu}+\mathbf{b})
+\tfrac12\mathbf{s}^\top(A\Sigma A^\top)\mathbf{s}$, so
$M_{\mathbf{w}}(\mathbf{s})=\exp\!\big(\mathbf{s}^\top(A\boldsymbol{\mu}+\mathbf{b})
+\tfrac12\mathbf{s}^\top(A\Sigma A^\top)\mathbf{s}\big)$, which is the moment generating function of
$\mathcal{N}_m(A\boldsymbol{\mu}+\mathbf{b},A\Sigma A^\top)$. By uniqueness of the moment generating
function, $\mathbf{w}$ has that distribution. $\square$
:::

::: {#lem-gaussian-block-independence}
## Uncorrelated Gaussian blocks are independent
Partition $\mathbf{u}=(\mathbf{u}_1,\mathbf{u}_2)$ jointly multivariate normal. If
$\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{u}_1,\mathbf{u}_2)=0$ then $\mathbf{u}_1$ and $\mathbf{u}_2$ are independent.
Consequently, measurable functions $f(\mathbf{u}_1)$ and $g(\mathbf{u}_2)$ are independent.
:::

::: {.proof}
Write $\mathbf{u}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\Sigma)$ with
$\boldsymbol{\mu}=(\boldsymbol{\mu}_1,\boldsymbol{\mu}_2)$ and, because the cross-covariance is zero,
the block-diagonal $\Sigma=\mathrm{diag}(\Sigma_{11},\Sigma_{22})$. For $\mathbf{t}=(\mathbf{t}_1,\mathbf{t}_2)$,
$$
M_{\mathbf{u}}(\mathbf{t})
=\exp\!\Big(\mathbf{t}_1^\top\boldsymbol{\mu}_1+\mathbf{t}_2^\top\boldsymbol{\mu}_2
+\tfrac12\mathbf{t}_1^\top\Sigma_{11}\mathbf{t}_1+\tfrac12\mathbf{t}_2^\top\Sigma_{22}\mathbf{t}_2\Big)
=M_{\mathbf{u}_1}(\mathbf{t}_1)\,M_{\mathbf{u}_2}(\mathbf{t}_2),
$$
the joint moment generating function factoring into the product of the marginal ones (each marginal is
normal by @lem-mvn-affine-closure with $A$ the appropriate coordinate projection). Factorization of the
joint moment generating function into the product of the marginals is equivalent to independence
(Chapter 4). Independence of $\mathbf{u}_1,\mathbf{u}_2$ implies independence of any measurable functions
$f(\mathbf{u}_1),g(\mathbf{u}_2)$. $\square$
:::

### The three distributional pillars

We can now read off the three pillars of normal regression theory. They are: $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$
is itself normal (the *location* information), the scaled residual sum of squares is chi-squared (the
*scale* information), and the two are independent (they do not interfere). Each is one line once the two
facts above are in hand.

::: {#thm-betahat-normal}
## Normality of the OLS estimator
Under @def-linear-model with G1, G2, G3 and $\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X})=p$,
$$
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\sim\mathcal{N}_p\big(\boldsymbol{\beta},\,\sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\big).
$$
:::

::: {.proof}
By G3, $\mathbf{y}\sim\mathcal{N}_n(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^2 I_n)$. The estimator
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=A\mathbf{y}$ with $A=(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top$ is an
affine (here, linear) function of $\mathbf{y}$. By @lem-mvn-affine-closure,
$$
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\sim\mathcal{N}_p\big(A\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta},\,\sigma^2 A A^\top\big).
$$
We computed $A\mathbf{X}=I_p$ and $\sigma^2 AA^\top=\sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}$ in
@thm-ols-moments, giving the claim. The mean and covariance agree with @eq-cov-betahat, as they must;
normality is the new information. $\square$
:::

**Why this matters.** Knowing $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ is exactly normal (not merely approximately) is
what lets us attach a confidence interval to a treatment effect from a single trial of finite size,
without appealing to large-sample approximation. It is the first ingredient of the $t$ statistic in
@thm-ttest.

The next theorem is the distributional heart of the chapter. Before stating it we isolate the
linear-algebra fact that is its true crux, so it has a name we can point to.

::: {#lem-idempotent-rank-trace}
## Rank of a symmetric idempotent equals its trace
Let $K\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ be symmetric and idempotent, $K=K^\top$ and $K^2=K$. Then every
eigenvalue of $K$ is $0$ or $1$, and the number of unit eigenvalues equals both $\mathrm{rank}(K)$ and
$\mathrm{tr}(K)$; in particular $\mathrm{rank}(K)=\mathrm{tr}(K)$.
:::

::: {.proof}
By the spectral theorem (@thm-spectral-theorem), $K=Q\Lambda Q^\top$ for an orthogonal $Q$ and a diagonal
$\Lambda$ holding the eigenvalues. Idempotence gives $Q\Lambda Q^\top=K=K^2=Q\Lambda^2 Q^\top$, so
$\Lambda^2=\Lambda$; entry by entry $\lambda_i^2=\lambda_i$, forcing $\lambda_i\in\{0,1\}$. The rank of
$K$ equals the number of nonzero eigenvalues (an orthogonal change of basis is invertible and preserves
rank), which is the number of ones; the trace is basis-independent and equals the sum of the eigenvalues,
again the number of ones. Hence $\mathrm{rank}(K)=\mathrm{tr}(K)$. $\square$
:::

**Reader translation.** For a projection matrix, counting dimensions and summing diagonal entries give
the same number. This is why $\mathrm{tr}(M)=n-p$ already told us the residual space has dimension $n-p$,
and it is exactly what fixes the chi-squared degrees of freedom below.

The argument now diagonalizes the residual maker by the spectral theorem and reduces the residual sum of
squares to a sum of independent squared standard normals.

**Roadmap of the proof.** The plan has four moves. (1) Write $\mathrm{RSS}=\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^\top
M\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$. (2) Diagonalize the symmetric idempotent $M$, whose eigenvalues are $0$ or $1$
with exactly $n-p$ ones (@lem-idempotent-rank-trace). (3) Rotate the noise by the orthogonal eigenvector
matrix; rotation keeps isotropic Gaussian noise standard normal. (4) In the rotated coordinates the
residual sum of squares is just the sum of the $n-p$ squared coordinates along the unit eigenvalues,
which is by definition a $\chi^2_{n-p}$.

::: {#thm-rss-chisq}
## Chi-squared distribution of the scaled residual sum of squares
Under @def-linear-model with G1, G2, G3 and $\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X})=p$ (and $n>p$),
$$
\frac{\mathrm{RSS}}{\sigma^2}=\frac{(n-p)s^2}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi^2_{\,n-p}.
$$
:::

::: {.proof}
As in @thm-sigma2-unbiased, $\mathrm{RSS}=\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^\top M\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$. The
matrix $M$ is symmetric, so by the spectral theorem (@thm-spectral-theorem) there is an orthogonal
matrix $Q$ ($Q^\top Q=QQ^\top=I_n$) and a diagonal matrix $\Lambda=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)$
with $M=Q\Lambda Q^\top$. By @lem-idempotent-rank-trace each eigenvalue is $0$ or $1$, and the number of
unit eigenvalues equals $\mathrm{rank}(M)=\mathrm{tr}(M)=n-p$. This is precisely *why* there are exactly
$n-p$ ones: the residual maker projects onto the $(n-p)$-dimensional residual space. Reorder the
eigenvalues so that $\Lambda=\mathrm{diag}(I_{n-p},0)$, with the $n-p$ ones first.

Define $\mathbf{z}=\sigma^{-1}Q^\top\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$. Since
$\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}_n(\mathbf{0},\sigma^2 I_n)$, @lem-mvn-affine-closure gives
$$
\mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{N}_n\big(\mathbf{0},\,\sigma^{-2}Q^\top(\sigma^2 I_n)Q\big)
=\mathcal{N}_n(\mathbf{0},Q^\top Q)=\mathcal{N}_n(\mathbf{0},I_n),
$$
so the coordinates $z_1,\dots,z_n$ are independent standard normal. From the definition of $\mathbf{z}$
we have $Q^\top\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}=\sigma\mathbf{z}$, so substituting $M=Q\Lambda Q^\top$,
$$
\frac{\mathrm{RSS}}{\sigma^2}
=\frac{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^\top M\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}{\sigma^2}
=\frac{(Q^\top\boldsymbol{\varepsilon})^\top\Lambda(Q^\top\boldsymbol{\varepsilon})}{\sigma^2}
=\frac{(\sigma\mathbf{z})^\top\Lambda(\sigma\mathbf{z})}{\sigma^2}
=\mathbf{z}^\top\Lambda\mathbf{z}=\sum_{i=1}^{n-p} z_i^2 .
$$
A sum of $n-p$ independent squared standard normal variables has, by definition, the chi-squared
distribution on $n-p$ degrees of freedom (Chapter 4). $\square$
:::

**Recap.** The rotation $Q$ turns the noise into $n$ independent standard-normal coordinates and turns
$M$ into a "keep the first $n-p$ directions, discard the other $p$" operator. The residual sum of squares
keeps only the kept coordinates, so it is a sum of $n-p$ squared independent standard normals.

```
   R^n  =  C(X)               +   C(X)^perp
           p directions            n-p directions
           (fitted lives here)     (residual lives here)

   rotate by Q:   noise -> n independent N(0,1) coordinates
   RSS / sigma^2  =  sum of the n-p squared coordinates in C(X)^perp  ->  chi^2_{n-p}
```

**Why this matters.** This theorem supplies the reference distribution for every variance-based test: the
$n-p$ denominator degrees of freedom in every $t$ and $F$ statistic later in the chapter trace back to
the dimension of the residual space counted here.

::: {#thm-betahat-s2-independence}
## Independence of the estimator and the variance estimate
Under @def-linear-model with G1, G2, G3 and $\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X})=p$, the random vector
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ and the statistic $s^2$ are independent. More generally
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ is independent of the entire residual vector $\mathbf{r}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Stack the fitted values and residuals into one affine function of $\mathbf{y}$:
$$
\begin{pmatrix}\hat{\mathbf{y}}\\ \mathbf{r}\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}H\\ M\end{pmatrix}\mathbf{y}.
$$
Since $\mathbf{y}$ is multivariate normal, @lem-mvn-affine-closure makes $(\hat{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{r})$
jointly multivariate normal. Their cross-covariance is
$$
\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{r})
=H\,\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{y})\,M^\top
=\sigma^2 H M=\sigma^2 H(I_n-H)=\sigma^2(H-H^2)=0,
$$
using $\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{y})=\sigma^2 I_n$ and $H^2=H$ (@lem-hat-properties). By
@lem-gaussian-block-independence, $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ and $\mathbf{r}$ are independent. Now
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}
=(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top H\mathbf{y}
=(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\hat{\mathbf{y}}$, using
$\mathbf{X}^\top H=\mathbf{X}^\top$, so $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ is a function of $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$
alone; and $s^2=\|\mathbf{r}\|_2^2/(n-p)$ is a function of $\mathbf{r}$ alone. Functions of independent
random vectors are independent (@lem-gaussian-block-independence), so $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ and
$s^2$ are independent, as is $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ from all of $\mathbf{r}$. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
The independence is special to the Gaussian case and is what makes exact finite-sample inference
possible. Geometrically, the orthogonal decomposition $\mathbf{y}=\hat{\mathbf{y}}+\mathbf{r}$ splits the
isotropic Gaussian noise into its components in $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$ and
$\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})^\perp$; the rotational symmetry of the isotropic normal makes those components
independent. The location information ($\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$) and the scale information ($s^2$) do
not interfere. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Exact inference: the t and F tests {#sec-lr-inference}

We assemble the pieces into *pivotal quantities*: functions of the data and one parameter whose sampling
distribution is completely known, free of every unknown parameter. A pivot is what turns an estimate into
a test or an interval, because we can tabulate its quantiles once and for all.
Recall from Chapter 4 the two constructions: if $Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ and $W\sim\chi^2_m$ are
independent then $Z/\sqrt{W/m}\sim t_m$ (Student's $t$ on $m$ degrees of freedom); and if
$W_1\sim\chi^2_{m_1}$ and $W_2\sim\chi^2_{m_2}$ are independent then
$(W_1/m_1)/(W_2/m_2)\sim F_{m_1,m_2}$ (Snedecor's $F$).

::: {#thm-ttest}
## The t statistic for a linear contrast
Assume @def-linear-model with G1, G2, G3 and $\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X})=p$, $n>p$. Fix
$\mathbf{c}\in\mathbb{R}^p\setminus\{\mathbf{0}\}$. Then
$$
T=\frac{\mathbf{c}^\top\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\mathbf{c}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}}
{s\sqrt{\mathbf{c}^\top(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{c}}}\sim t_{\,n-p}.
$$ {#eq-ttest}
In particular, taking $\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{e}_j$ gives the per-coefficient statistic
$T_j=(\hat\beta_j-\beta_j)/\big(s\sqrt{[(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}]_{jj}}\big)\sim t_{\,n-p}$, and a
level $1-\alpha$ confidence interval for $\beta_j$ is
$\hat\beta_j\pm t_{n-p,1-\alpha/2}\,s\sqrt{[(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}]_{jj}}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
By @thm-betahat-normal and the linear-image rule for the normal (the scalar case of
@lem-mvn-affine-closure), $\mathbf{c}^\top\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\sim
\mathcal{N}\big(\mathbf{c}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^2\mathbf{c}^\top(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{c}\big)$.
The denominator variance is positive because $(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}$ is positive definite
(@lem-gram-nullspace) and $\mathbf{c}\ne\mathbf{0}$. Standardize:
$$
Z=\frac{\mathbf{c}^\top\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\mathbf{c}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}}
{\sigma\sqrt{\mathbf{c}^\top(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{c}}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1).
$$
By @thm-rss-chisq, $W=\mathrm{RSS}/\sigma^2=(n-p)s^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2_{n-p}$. By
@thm-betahat-s2-independence, $Z$ (a function of $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$) is independent of $W$ (a
function of $s^2$). Therefore
$$
\frac{Z}{\sqrt{W/(n-p)}}\sim t_{\,n-p}.
$$
Substituting $W/(n-p)=s^2/\sigma^2$, the unknown $\sigma$ cancels:
$$
\frac{Z}{\sqrt{W/(n-p)}}
=\frac{(\mathbf{c}^\top\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\mathbf{c}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta})\big/
\big(\sigma\sqrt{\mathbf{c}^\top(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{c}}\big)}{s/\sigma}
=\frac{\mathbf{c}^\top\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\mathbf{c}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}}
{s\sqrt{\mathbf{c}^\top(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{c}}}=T,
$$
which is @eq-ttest. The confidence interval is the set of $\beta_j$ for which $|T_j|\le t_{n-p,1-\alpha/2}$,
obtained by inverting the two-sided test. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reading the quantile notation.** The symbol $t_{n-p,1-\alpha/2}$ is the number with probability
$1-\alpha/2$ to its left under the $t_{n-p}$ curve; for a $95\%$ interval ($\alpha=0.05$) it cuts off the
top $2.5\%$ of the curve, so the interval misses the truth at most $5\%$ of the time. It is the
`qt(1 - alpha/2, n - p)` of statistical software. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

**Why this matters (health reading).** The per-coefficient statistic $T_j$ is exactly the $t$ value a
regression table prints for each covariate, and
$\hat\beta_j\pm t_{n-p,1-\alpha/2}\,s\sqrt{[(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}]_{jj}}$ is its confidence
interval. Choosing $\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{e}_T$, the treatment column, gives the test and interval for the
adjusted treatment effect, the headline number of a trial analysis.

For testing several coefficients at once we compare nested models. Let $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}_0)\subseteq
\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}_1)$ be the column spaces of a reduced design $\mathbf{X}_0$ (with $p_0$ columns,
full rank) and a full design $\mathbf{X}_1$ (with $p_1>p_0$ columns, full rank, $n>p_1$), with hat
matrices $H_0,H_1$, residual makers $M_0,M_1$, and residual sums of squares $\mathrm{RSS}_0,\mathrm{RSS}_1$.

::: {#thm-ftest}
## The F statistic for nested models
Assume G1, G2, G3 and that the reduced model holds, that is,
$\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{y}]\in\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}_0)$. With $q=p_1-p_0$,
$$
F=\frac{(\mathrm{RSS}_0-\mathrm{RSS}_1)/q}{\mathrm{RSS}_1/(n-p_1)}\sim F_{\,q,\;n-p_1}.
$$ {#eq-fstat}
:::

**Roadmap of the proof.** Two nested models differ by $q=p_1-p_0$ extra columns. The drop in residual
sum of squares, $\mathrm{RSS}_0-\mathrm{RSS}_1$, measures what those extra columns explain. We show this
drop equals $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^\top P\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$ for a projection $P$ of rank $q$
onto the "extra" directions, that $\mathrm{RSS}_1=\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^\top M_1
\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$ lives on the orthogonal residual directions, and that the two are independent
chi-squares; their scaled ratio is then an $F$ by construction.

::: {.proof}
Because $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}_0)\subseteq\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}_1)$, projecting onto the smaller space
and then the larger leaves the smaller projection unchanged: $H_1H_0=H_0H_1=H_0$. (Indeed
$H_1H_0$ projects each column of $H_0$, which already lies in $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}_0)\subseteq
\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}_1)$, onto $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}_1)$, returning it unchanged; symmetry gives the
other equality.) Define the difference $P=H_1-H_0$. Then $P$ is symmetric and
$$
P^2=(H_1-H_0)^2=H_1-H_1H_0-H_0H_1+H_0=H_1-H_0-H_0+H_0=H_1-H_0=P,
$$
where the four-term expansion used $H_1^2=H_1$, $H_0^2=H_0$, and the identity $H_1H_0=H_0H_1=H_0$ just
established. So $P$ is symmetric and idempotent, hence an orthogonal projection, and by
@lem-idempotent-rank-trace its rank equals its trace,
$\mathrm{rank}(P)=\mathrm{tr}(P)=\mathrm{tr}(H_1)-\mathrm{tr}(H_0)=p_1-p_0=q$. Moreover $P$ and
$M_1=I-H_1$ are orthogonal projections whose product is zero:
$$
PM_1=(H_1-H_0)(I-H_1)=H_1-H_1^2-H_0+H_0H_1=H_1-H_1-H_0+H_0=0 .
$$
Because $P$ and $M_1$ are symmetric projections with $PM_1=0$, their ranges are orthogonal subspaces of
$\mathbb{R}^n$; this orthogonality is exactly the condition that, applied to Gaussian noise, will make
the two pieces $P\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$ and $M_1\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$ independent below. Now
decompose the numerator. Using $\mathrm{RSS}_k=\mathbf{y}^\top M_k\mathbf{y}$,
$$
\mathrm{RSS}_0-\mathrm{RSS}_1=\mathbf{y}^\top(M_0-M_1)\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{y}^\top(H_1-H_0)\mathbf{y}
=\mathbf{y}^\top P\mathbf{y}.
$$
Write $\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{X}_0\boldsymbol{\beta}_0+\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$ under the reduced model.
Because $P\mathbf{X}_0=H_1\mathbf{X}_0-H_0\mathbf{X}_0=\mathbf{X}_0-\mathbf{X}_0=0$ (both projections fix
$\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}_0)$), we get $P\mathbf{y}=P\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$ and likewise
$M_1\mathbf{y}=M_1\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$. Hence
$$
\mathrm{RSS}_0-\mathrm{RSS}_1=\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^\top P\boldsymbol{\varepsilon},
\qquad
\mathrm{RSS}_1=\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^\top M_1\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}.
$$
By the spectral argument of @thm-rss-chisq applied to the idempotent $P$ of rank $q$ and to $M_1$ of
rank $n-p_1$,
$$
\frac{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^\top P\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi^2_q,
\qquad
\frac{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^\top M_1\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi^2_{n-p_1}.
$$
For independence, stack $P\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$ and $M_1\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$; they are jointly
normal (@lem-mvn-affine-closure) with cross-covariance
$\mathrm{Cov}(P\boldsymbol{\varepsilon},M_1\boldsymbol{\varepsilon})=\sigma^2 PM_1=0$, so by
@lem-gaussian-block-independence the two random vectors are independent, and therefore so are the
quadratic forms $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^\top P\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$ and
$\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^\top M_1\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$ built from them. The ratio of independent
chi-squared variables, each divided by its degrees of freedom, is
$$
F=\frac{(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^\top P\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}/\sigma^2)/q}
{(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^\top M_1\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}/\sigma^2)/(n-p_1)}
=\frac{(\mathrm{RSS}_0-\mathrm{RSS}_1)/q}{\mathrm{RSS}_1/(n-p_1)}\sim F_{\,q,\;n-p_1},
$$
the unknown $\sigma^2$ cancelling. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
Taking $\mathbf{X}_0=\mathbf{1}_n$ (intercept only, $p_0=1$) tests the global null that all slopes are
zero. Then $H_0\mathbf{y}=\bar y\,\mathbf{1}_n$, $H_1\mathbf{y}=\hat{\mathbf{y}}$, and the numerator
quadratic form is $\|(H_1-H_0)\mathbf{y}\|_2^2=\|\hat{\mathbf{y}}-\bar y\mathbf{1}_n\|_2^2
=\mathrm{ESS}_{\mathrm{reg}}$, so
$$
F=\frac{\mathrm{ESS}_{\mathrm{reg}}/(p-1)}{\mathrm{RSS}/(n-p)}\sim F_{\,p-1,\;n-p}
$$
under the null. When $q=1$ the $F$ statistic equals the square of the corresponding $t$ statistic,
$F=T^2$, and $F_{1,m}$ is the law of the square of a $t_m$ variable; the two tests then agree. The
general linear hypothesis $H_0:R\boldsymbol{\beta}=\mathbf{q}$ for a full-row-rank $R\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times p}$
gives an algebraically equivalent statistic, which we state and prove as @thm-general-linear-hypothesis
below because it is the form practitioners actually use. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

**Why this matters (health reading).** The global-null $F$ asks whether the regressors together explain
more than chance: in the running trial, whether treatment and baseline severity jointly beat an
intercept-only model. The "F-statistic" line of a regression printout is exactly this test. The
nested-model view also matches how covariates are added to a model one block at a time, each block tested
by the drop in residual sum of squares it produces.

The nested-model $F$ test of @thm-ftest is often more convenient to express directly in terms of a
restriction on the coefficients. The next theorem gives that form. It is worth a full statement, not a
passing remark, because it is the test computed by routines such as `linearHypothesis()` in R.

::: {#thm-general-linear-hypothesis}
## The general linear hypothesis
Assume @def-linear-model with G1, G2, G3 and $\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X})=p$, $n>p$. Let
$R\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times p}$ have full row rank $q\le p$, and let $\mathbf{q}\in\mathbb{R}^q$. Under the
null hypothesis $H_0:R\boldsymbol{\beta}=\mathbf{q}$,
$$
F=\frac{(R\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\mathbf{q})^\top\big[R(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}R^\top\big]^{-1}
(R\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\mathbf{q})}{q\,s^2}\sim F_{q,\,n-p}.
$$ {#eq-glh-stat}
:::

::: {.proof}
Write $A=R(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}R^\top$. Since $R$ has full row rank and
$(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}$ is positive definite (@lem-gram-nullspace), $A$ is a $q\times q$
positive definite, hence invertible, matrix. By @thm-betahat-normal and affine closure
(@lem-mvn-affine-closure), $R\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\sim\mathcal{N}_q(R\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^2 A)$, so
under $H_0$ the vector $\mathbf{v}:=R\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\mathbf{q}\sim\mathcal{N}_q(\mathbf{0},
\sigma^2 A)$.

We now *whiten* $\mathbf{v}$, that is, transform it to have the identity covariance. Factor $A=LL^\top$
(for example the Cholesky factor, or $A^{1/2}$ from the spectral theorem, @thm-spectral-theorem) and set
$\mathbf{u}=\sigma^{-1}L^{-1}\mathbf{v}$. By @lem-mvn-affine-closure,
$$
\mathbf{u}\sim\mathcal{N}_q\big(\mathbf{0},\,\sigma^{-2}L^{-1}(\sigma^2 A)L^{-\top}\big)
=\mathcal{N}_q\big(\mathbf{0},\,L^{-1}LL^\top L^{-\top}\big)=\mathcal{N}_q(\mathbf{0},I_q),
$$
so the coordinates of $\mathbf{u}$ are independent standard normals and
$$
\frac{\mathbf{v}^\top A^{-1}\mathbf{v}}{\sigma^2}=\mathbf{u}^\top\mathbf{u}
=\sum_{i=1}^q u_i^2\sim\chi^2_q .
$$
By @thm-rss-chisq, $W:=(n-p)s^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2_{n-p}$, and by @thm-betahat-s2-independence the
numerator (a function of $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$) is independent of $s^2$. Hence
$$
\frac{\big(\mathbf{v}^\top A^{-1}\mathbf{v}/\sigma^2\big)/q}{W/(n-p)}
=\frac{\mathbf{v}^\top A^{-1}\mathbf{v}}{q\,s^2}
=\frac{(R\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\mathbf{q})^\top A^{-1}(R\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\mathbf{q})}{q\,s^2}
\sim F_{q,\,n-p},
$$
the unknown $\sigma^2$ cancelling. This is @eq-glh-stat. $\square$
:::

**Why this matters (ITC).** This statistic tests any set of $q$ linear restrictions at once, for example
"treatment has no effect at any dose" or "two treatment contrasts are equal." In network meta-analysis,
joint restrictions on treatment contrasts are exactly the hypotheses of interest. @exr-lr-general-hypothesis
asks you to check that @eq-glh-stat coincides with the nested-model statistic @eq-fstat.

## Decomposition of variance and the coefficient of determination {#sec-lr-anova}

The Pythagorean identity of @prp-fitted-residual-geometry, applied to the *centered* response, splits
the total variability of $\mathbf{y}$ into a part explained by the regression and a residual part. This
is the analysis of variance, and it gives the most-quoted summary of fit.

::: {#prp-anova-decomposition}
## Analysis-of-variance decomposition
Assume the model contains an intercept, $\mathbf{1}_n\in\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$. Then the fitted values
and residuals are orthogonal after centering, and
$$
\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\bar y)^2}_{\mathrm{TSS}}
=\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n (\hat y_i-\bar y)^2}_{\mathrm{ESS}_{\mathrm{reg}}}
+\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\hat y_i)^2}_{\mathrm{RSS}} .
$$ {#eq-anova}
:::

::: {.proof}
Center the identity $\mathbf{y}=\hat{\mathbf{y}}+\mathbf{r}$ by subtracting $\bar y\mathbf{1}_n$:
$$
\mathbf{y}-\bar y\mathbf{1}_n=(\hat{\mathbf{y}}-\bar y\mathbf{1}_n)+\mathbf{r},
$$
where we used $\overline{\hat y}=\bar y$, valid because the model has an intercept
(@prp-fitted-residual-geometry). The two summands on the right are orthogonal: the residual
$\mathbf{r}=M\mathbf{y}\in\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})^\perp$, while
$\hat{\mathbf{y}}-\bar y\mathbf{1}_n\in\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$ because both $\hat{\mathbf{y}}=H\mathbf{y}$
and $\mathbf{1}_n$ lie in $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$. Hence
$(\hat{\mathbf{y}}-\bar y\mathbf{1}_n)^\top\mathbf{r}=0$, and the Pythagorean theorem yields
$$
\|\mathbf{y}-\bar y\mathbf{1}_n\|_2^2
=\|\hat{\mathbf{y}}-\bar y\mathbf{1}_n\|_2^2+\|\mathbf{r}\|_2^2,
$$
which is @eq-anova in vector form. $\square$
:::

The decomposition is a right triangle on the centered vectors, with the right angle at $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$.

```
              y
             /|
            / |
   TSS    /   |  RSS            TSS     = squared length of the hypotenuse
  (hyp)  /    |  (leg)          ESS_reg = squared length of the horizontal leg
        /     |                 RSS     = squared length of the vertical leg
       /______|
   ybar*1   yhat
       ESS_reg (leg)

   right angle at yhat:   TSS = ESS_reg + RSS
```

**Reader translation.** Total variation in the response splits into the part the model explains
($\mathrm{ESS}_{\mathrm{reg}}$) plus the part it cannot ($\mathrm{RSS}$), and because the two are at right
angles, the split is exact (no cross term). $R^2$, defined next, is simply the explained fraction of the
hypotenuse, so a larger $R^2$ means the explained leg is the longer share of the triangle.

::: {#def-r-squared}
## Coefficient of determination
For a model with intercept and $\mathrm{TSS}>0$, the **coefficient of determination** is
$$
R^2=\frac{\mathrm{ESS}_{\mathrm{reg}}}{\mathrm{TSS}}=1-\frac{\mathrm{RSS}}{\mathrm{TSS}},
$$
the fraction of the total (centered) variability of the response explained by the regression. The two
expressions are equal by @prp-anova-decomposition. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

**Reader translation.** $R^2$ is the share of the response's spread the model accounts for: $R^2=0.64$
means the regressors explain $64\%$ of the variability and $36\%$ is residual scatter. It measures fit,
not correctness or causation; a high $R^2$ does not make a treatment-effect estimate unbiased, and a low
one does not make it wrong.

::: {#cor-rsquared-range}
## Range and correlation interpretation of R squared
For a model with intercept, $0\le R^2\le 1$. The value $R^2=1$ occurs exactly when all residuals vanish
($\mathbf{y}\in\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$) and $R^2=0$ exactly when $\hat{\mathbf{y}}=\bar y\mathbf{1}_n$
(the regressors add nothing beyond the intercept). In simple linear regression
($\mathbf{X}=[\mathbf{1}_n\ \mathbf{x}]$, $p=2$), $R^2=\rho_{xy}^2$, the square of the sample
correlation $\rho_{xy}=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)\big/\sqrt{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
From @eq-anova, $\mathrm{TSS}=\mathrm{ESS}_{\mathrm{reg}}+\mathrm{RSS}$ with both summands nonnegative,
so $0\le\mathrm{ESS}_{\mathrm{reg}}\le\mathrm{TSS}$ and dividing by $\mathrm{TSS}>0$ gives $0\le R^2\le1$.
The boundary cases are read directly from $R^2=1-\mathrm{RSS}/\mathrm{TSS}$ and
$R^2=\mathrm{ESS}_{\mathrm{reg}}/\mathrm{TSS}$.

For simple linear regression, the slope estimator is
$\hat\beta_1=S_{xy}/S_{xx}$ with $S_{xy}=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)$ and
$S_{xx}=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2$ (the specialization of @eq-normal-equations to $p=2$; see
@exr-lr-simple-formulas). Since $\hat y_i-\bar y=\hat\beta_1(x_i-\bar x)$,
$$
\mathrm{ESS}_{\mathrm{reg}}=\sum_i(\hat y_i-\bar y)^2=\hat\beta_1^2 S_{xx}=\frac{S_{xy}^2}{S_{xx}},
\qquad
R^2=\frac{\mathrm{ESS}_{\mathrm{reg}}}{\mathrm{TSS}}=\frac{S_{xy}^2}{S_{xx}S_{yy}}=\rho_{xy}^2,
$$
with $S_{yy}=\mathrm{TSS}=\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2$. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality (@thm-cauchy-schwarz-ip)
applied to the centered vectors $\mathbf{x}-\bar x\mathbf{1}_n$ and $\mathbf{y}-\bar y\mathbf{1}_n$ gives
$S_{xy}^2\le S_{xx}S_{yy}$, confirming $0\le\rho_{xy}^2\le 1$ once more. $\square$
:::

## Least squares is maximum likelihood {#sec-lr-mle}

We have introduced least squares as a geometric and decision-theoretic object, and shown it is best in
two senses (closest point; BLUE). Under normal errors there is a third, statistical justification that
many find the most compelling: minimizing the sum of squares is exactly maximizing the likelihood. This
is the answer to "why squares" promised in the introduction: squaring is the price of assuming the noise
is Gaussian. Had we instead assumed Laplace-shaped (double-exponential) noise, the likelihood would
reward *absolute* residuals, and the estimator would minimize the sum of absolute deviations. The squared
criterion is thus a modeling choice about the shape of the noise, now made explicit.

### Ordinary least squares is the maximum likelihood estimator

::: {#thm-ols-mle-normal}
## Least squares is maximum likelihood under normal errors
Assume @def-linear-model with G1, G2, G3 and $\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X})=p$, $n>p$, treating
$(\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^2)$ as unknown parameters. The maximum likelihood estimators are
$$
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathrm{MLE}}=(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}
=\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathrm{OLS}},
\qquad
\hat\sigma^2_{\mathrm{MLE}}=\frac{\mathrm{RSS}}{n}.
$$
That is, the maximum likelihood estimator of $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is precisely the ordinary
least-squares estimator. (The maximum likelihood estimator of $\sigma^2$ uses divisor $n$, not $n-p$,
and is therefore biased downward; compare @thm-sigma2-unbiased.)
:::

::: {.proof}
Under G3 the density of $\mathbf{y}\sim\mathcal{N}_n(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^2 I_n)$ is
$(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}\exp\!\big(-\|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_2^2/(2\sigma^2)\big)$, so
the log-likelihood is
$$
\ell(\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^2)
=-\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi)-\frac{n}{2}\log\sigma^2
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\,\|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_2^2 .
$$ {#eq-loglik}
For any fixed $\sigma^2>0$, the only place $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ enters @eq-loglik is through the term
$-\|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_2^2/(2\sigma^2)$, which is increasing in
$-S(\boldsymbol{\beta})$. Maximizing $\ell$ over $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is therefore identical to
minimizing $S(\boldsymbol{\beta})=\|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_2^2$, whose unique
minimizer is the OLS estimator $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top
\mathbf{y}$ by @thm-ols-normal-equations. Crucially, this minimizing $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ is the
*same* for every fixed $\sigma^2>0$: the factor $1/(2\sigma^2)$ only rescales the term it multiplies and
