does not move the location of the minimum. Because the best $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is the same whatever
$\sigma^2$ is, that same $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ must be the $\boldsymbol{\beta}$-coordinate of the
joint maximizer over $(\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^2)$. Substituting $\boldsymbol{\beta}=\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$
back into $\ell$ leaves a function of $\sigma^2$ alone, the **profile log-likelihood** (the likelihood
with the other parameter concentrated out at its optimal value),
$$
\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\sigma^2)
=-\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi)-\frac{n}{2}\log\sigma^2-\frac{\mathrm{RSS}}{2\sigma^2},
$$
where $\mathrm{RSS}=\|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\|_2^2>0$ almost surely (it is zero only
on the measure-zero event $\mathbf{y}\in\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$). Differentiate in $\sigma^2$:
$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial\sigma^2}\,\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\sigma^2)
=-\frac{n}{2\sigma^2}+\frac{\mathrm{RSS}}{2\sigma^4}
=\frac{1}{2\sigma^4}\big(\mathrm{RSS}-n\sigma^2\big),
$$
which is positive for $\sigma^2<\mathrm{RSS}/n$, zero at $\sigma^2=\mathrm{RSS}/n$, and negative for
$\sigma^2>\mathrm{RSS}/n$. Hence $\sigma^2\mapsto\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\sigma^2)$ increases then
decreases, with a unique global maximum at $\hat\sigma^2_{\mathrm{MLE}}=\mathrm{RSS}/n$. Therefore
$(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\mathrm{RSS}/n)$ maximizes $\ell$ jointly. $\square$
:::

**Why this matters.** This is the third of the four optimality principles from the introduction, and the
one that justifies the squared-error criterion by name: under Gaussian errors, least squares is the
maximum likelihood estimator, not an arbitrary choice. It also hooks regression into the general
machinery of Chapter 5, so the large-sample guarantees of maximum likelihood apply to
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ automatically.

### Cramér-Rao efficiency

Under normality we can say more than Gauss-Markov: $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ is optimal not merely among
linear unbiased estimators but among *all* unbiased estimators, because it attains the Cramér-Rao lower
bound (@thm-cramer-rao).

::: {#cor-ols-efficient-normal}
## OLS attains the Cramér-Rao bound under normality
Assume G1, G2, G3 and $\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X})=p$, with $\sigma^2$ known. The Fisher information
(@def-fisher-information) for $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is
$\mathcal{I}(\boldsymbol{\beta})=\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}/\sigma^2$. Consequently, for every fixed
$\mathbf{c}\in\mathbb{R}^p$, any unbiased estimator $T$ of $\mathbf{c}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}$ satisfies
$\mathrm{Var}(T)\ge\sigma^2\mathbf{c}^\top(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{c}
=\mathrm{Var}(\mathbf{c}^\top\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})$. The OLS estimator
$\mathbf{c}^\top\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ is therefore the uniformly minimum variance unbiased estimator
of $\mathbf{c}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
With $\sigma^2$ known, drop the additive constants in @eq-loglik that do not involve
$\boldsymbol{\beta}$; the score is
$$
\mathbf{s}(\boldsymbol{\beta})=\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\,\ell
=\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\mathbf{X}^\top(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}),
$$
with Hessian $\nabla^2_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\ell=-\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}/\sigma^2$, a constant matrix.
The Fisher information is minus the expected Hessian, so
$\mathcal{I}(\boldsymbol{\beta})=\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}/\sigma^2$. The Cramér-Rao inequality
(@thm-cramer-rao), in its form for a smooth scalar functional $\psi(\boldsymbol{\beta})
=\mathbf{c}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}$ with gradient $\mathbf{c}$, gives for any unbiased $T$
$$
\mathrm{Var}(T)\ge\mathbf{c}^\top\mathcal{I}(\boldsymbol{\beta})^{-1}\mathbf{c}
=\sigma^2\,\mathbf{c}^\top(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{c}.
$$
By @thm-ols-moments the right-hand side equals $\mathrm{Var}(\mathbf{c}^\top\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})$,
so the bound is attained by OLS, which is unbiased; no unbiased estimator can do better. The same
conclusion holds when $\sigma^2$ is unknown: the information matrix for $(\boldsymbol{\beta},\sigma^2)$ is
block diagonal, because $\partial^2\ell/\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}\,\partial\sigma^2
=-\sigma^{-4}\mathbf{X}^\top(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})$ has expectation $\mathbf{0}$ under
G1. A block-diagonal matrix is inverted block by block, so the $\boldsymbol{\beta}$-block of the inverse
information is simply the inverse of the $\boldsymbol{\beta}$-block of the information, namely
$\sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}$. In words: not knowing $\sigma^2$ costs nothing for estimating
$\boldsymbol{\beta}$, so the same lower bound persists. $\square$
:::

**Why this matters.** This is the strongest optimality statement in the chapter, the fourth principle of
the introduction. Gauss-Markov ruled out only *linear* rivals; Cramér-Rao rules out *all* unbiased
rivals, even nonlinear ones, once we assume normality. For a health researcher the practical reading is
that under its assumptions there is no cleverer unbiased way to estimate a treatment effect than ordinary
least squares; effort is better spent checking the assumptions than seeking a better estimator.

::: {.remark}
Three optimality theorems now point to the same estimator. Gauss-Markov (@thm-ols-blue) selects OLS
among linear unbiased estimators using only the first two moments; the projection theorem selects it as
the closest point in the model space using only geometry; @cor-ols-efficient-normal selects it among all
unbiased estimators under the added assumption of normality. When the errors are heavy-tailed or the
model is misspecified these justifications weaken, and the robust sandwich variance of
@def-sandwich-variance, or estimators based on other loss functions, become relevant. The large-sample
guarantees of @thm-mle-asymptotic-normality apply to $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ as a maximum likelihood
estimator and extend the normal-theory exact results to settings where G3 holds only approximately.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Rank deficiency and the pseudoinverse {#sec-lr-rank}

When the columns of $\mathbf{X}$ are linearly dependent, for example because a categorical predictor is
coded with one indicator per level together with an intercept, $\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X})=q<p$ and
$\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}$ is singular. The formula @eq-betahat no longer applies, but the geometry
survives intact: the fitted values are still the unique projection of $\mathbf{y}$ onto
$\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$, and only the coordinate representation $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is
non-unique. The clean device for selecting a canonical representative is the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse
$\mathbf{X}^{+}$ (@def-pseudoinverse), built from the singular value decomposition (@thm-svd).

The four fundamental subspaces (@thm-four-subspaces) each acquire a regression meaning, summarized here.
The two on the left of the table live in observation space $\mathbb{R}^n$; the two on the right live in
coefficient space $\mathbb{R}^p$ and govern identifiability.

| Subspace | Where | Dimension | Regression meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$, column space | $\mathbb{R}^n$ | $\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X})$ | where fitted values $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ live (the model space) |
| $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})^\perp=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X}^\top)$ | $\mathbb{R}^n$ | $n-\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X})$ | where residuals $\mathbf{r}$ live |
| $\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X})$, null space | $\mathbb{R}^p$ | $p-\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X})$ | directions in which $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is undetermined (non-identifiable) |
| $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}^\top)$, row space | $\mathbb{R}^p$ | $\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X})$ | directions $\mathbf{c}$ along which $\mathbf{c}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is estimable |

The last row gives a name to the central concept of this section.

::: {#def-estimable}
## Estimable functional
A linear functional $\mathbf{c}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is **estimable** if it takes the same value for
every least-squares solution $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ of the normal equations @eq-normal-equations.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

**Reader translation.** When the design is rank deficient, infinitely many coefficient vectors fit the
data equally well, so an individual coefficient can be meaningless on its own: it changes from one
solution to another. An estimable functional is a combination that *does* have a single well-defined
value, whichever solution the software returns. @prp-rank-deficient-pseudoinverse shows these are exactly
the combinations $\mathbf{c}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}$ with $\mathbf{c}\in\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}^\top)$. A
treatment contrast is typically estimable even when the separate arm intercepts are not, which is why a
difference between treatments is reportable from a design that cannot pin down each arm's absolute level.

::: {#prp-rank-deficient-pseudoinverse}
## Rank deficiency and the minimum-norm solution
Let $\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X})=q\le p$. Then:

1. The normal equations @eq-normal-equations are consistent, and their solution set is the affine
   subspace $\{\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_0+\mathbf{v}:\mathbf{v}\in\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X})\}$ for any
   particular solution $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_0$.
2. The fitted values $\hat{\mathbf{y}}=\mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=P_{\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})}\mathbf{y}$
   and the residual $\mathbf{r}$ are the same for every solution; hence so is $\mathrm{RSS}$, and a
   linear functional $\mathbf{c}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is invariant across solutions if and only if
   $\mathbf{c}\in\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}^\top)$ (these are exactly the **estimable** functionals of
   @def-estimable).
3. Among all minimizers, the one of smallest Euclidean norm is unique and equals
   $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{+}=\mathbf{X}^{+}\mathbf{y}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
(1) Consistency was shown in @thm-ols-normal-equations: $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}\in
\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}^\top)=\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})$ by @lem-gram-nullspace, so a solution
exists. If $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_0$ and $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_1$ both solve the normal equations
then $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_1-\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_0)=\mathbf{0}$, so
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_1-\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_0\in\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})
=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X})$ (@lem-gram-nullspace); conversely adding any
$\mathbf{v}\in\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X})$ to a solution gives another solution. This is the stated affine
subspace.

(2) The projection theorem (@thm-projection-theorem) gives a *unique* closest point $\hat{\mathbf{y}}
=P_{\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})}\mathbf{y}\in\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$ regardless of coordinates; any solution
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ satisfies $\mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ because
solving the normal equations is equivalent to $\mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ being that projection
(the orthogonality $\mathbf{X}^\top(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\mathbf{0}$). Hence
$\hat{\mathbf{y}}$, $\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ and $\mathrm{RSS}=\|\mathbf{r}\|_2^2$ are
solution-independent. For a functional, $\mathbf{c}^\top\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ is invariant across
solutions iff $\mathbf{c}^\top\mathbf{v}=0$ for all $\mathbf{v}\in\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X})$, that is iff
$\mathbf{c}\in\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X})^\perp=\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}^\top)$ (@thm-four-subspaces).

(3) Take a (thin) singular value decomposition $\mathbf{X}=U\Sigma V^\top$ (@thm-svd) with $U\in
\mathbb{R}^{n\times q}$, $V\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times q}$ having orthonormal columns and
$\Sigma=\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_q)$, $\sigma_i>0$. The pseudoinverse is
$\mathbf{X}^{+}=V\Sigma^{-1}U^\top$, and $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{+}=\mathbf{X}^{+}\mathbf{y}=V\Sigma^{-1}U^\top\mathbf{y}
\in\mathcal{C}(V)=\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}^\top)=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X})^\perp$. One checks
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{+}$ solves the normal equations: $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{+}=V\Sigma^2 V^\top V\Sigma^{-1}U^\top\mathbf{y}=V\Sigma U^\top\mathbf{y}
=\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}$. Any other solution is $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{+}+\mathbf{v}$ with
$\mathbf{v}\in\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X})$ by part (1); since
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{+}\in\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X})^\perp\perp\mathbf{v}$, Pythagoras gives
$\|\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{+}+\mathbf{v}\|_2^2=\|\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{+}\|_2^2+\|\mathbf{v}\|_2^2
\ge\|\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{+}\|_2^2$, with equality only at $\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$. So
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{+}$ is the unique minimum-norm minimizer. $\square$
:::

**Why this matters (ITC).** Estimability is the linear-algebra skeleton of identification in indirect
comparison. A network of trials defines a design on the treatment contrasts, and which contrasts the
network can estimate is exactly the estimability question of part (2). We return to it for network
meta-analysis in Part III.

::: {.remark}
In the full-rank case $q=p$ the null space is trivial, every functional is estimable, the affine
solution set collapses to the single point @eq-betahat, and $\mathbf{X}^{+}=(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}
\mathbf{X}^\top$, so @prp-rank-deficient-pseudoinverse reduces to the earlier theory. The estimability
criterion in part (2) is the rigorous statement of which contrasts a rank-deficient design can identify;
in network meta-analysis and population adjustment the analogous question, which treatment contrasts a
design renders estimable, is central, and reappears in Part III. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## A fully worked example {#sec-lr-example}

We carry a small data set through every formula so the reader can verify each number by hand. To give it
a clinical reading, interpret $x$ as a patient's **baseline disease severity score** and $y$ as the
**change in a continuous symptom outcome** over follow-up, for $n=5$ patients, fit with intercept
($p=2$):
$$
\mathbf{x}=(1,2,3,4,5)^\top,\qquad \mathbf{y}=(1,3,2,5,4)^\top,\qquad
\mathbf{X}=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&2\\1&3\\1&4\\1&5\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**Summary statistics.** We have $\sum x_i=15$, $\sum x_i^2=55$, $\sum y_i=15$, $\sum x_iy_i=53$, hence
$\bar x=\bar y=3$, $S_{xx}=\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2=10$, $S_{yy}=\sum(y_i-\bar y)^2=10$, and
$S_{xy}=\sum(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)=8$.

**The Gram matrix and its inverse.**
$$
\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}=\begin{pmatrix}n&\sum x_i\\ \sum x_i&\sum x_i^2\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}5&15\\15&55\end{pmatrix},\quad
\det(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})=5\cdot55-15^2=50,\quad
(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}=\frac{1}{50}\begin{pmatrix}55&-15\\-15&5\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}1.1&-0.3\\-0.3&0.1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**The estimate.** With $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}=(\sum y_i,\sum x_iy_i)^\top=(15,53)^\top$,
$$
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}
=\begin{pmatrix}1.1&-0.3\\-0.3&0.1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}15\\53\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}1.1(15)-0.3(53)\\-0.3(15)+0.1(53)\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}16.5-15.9\\-4.5+5.3\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0.6\\0.8\end{pmatrix}.
$$
Equivalently, by the simple-regression formulas, $\hat\beta_1=S_{xy}/S_{xx}=8/10=0.8$ and
$\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x=3-0.8\cdot3=0.6$. The fitted line is $\hat y=0.6+0.8x$. Clinically,
the slope $\hat\beta_1=0.8$ says each additional point of baseline severity is associated with a
$0.8$-unit larger change in the outcome, and the intercept $\hat\beta_0=0.6$ is the predicted change at a
(hypothetical) severity of zero.

**Fitted values and residuals.**
$$
\hat{\mathbf{y}}=(1.4,\,2.2,\,3.0,\,3.8,\,4.6)^\top,\qquad
\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}}=(-0.4,\,0.8,\,-1.0,\,1.2,\,-0.6)^\top.
$$
As @prp-fitted-residual-geometry predicts, $\sum_i r_i=0$ and $\sum_i x_i r_i=0$ (the two normal
equations); the reader can check both sums are exactly zero. A residual such as $r_4=1.2$ means patient
$4$'s observed change exceeded the model's prediction by $1.2$ units.

**Sums of squares and $R^2$.**
$$
\mathrm{RSS}=\sum r_i^2=0.16+0.64+1.00+1.44+0.36=3.6,\quad
\mathrm{TSS}=S_{yy}=10,\quad
\mathrm{ESS}_{\mathrm{reg}}=10-3.6=6.4,
$$
in agreement with $\mathrm{ESS}_{\mathrm{reg}}=\hat\beta_1^2 S_{xx}=0.64\cdot10=6.4$ and the ANOVA
identity @eq-anova: $10=6.4+3.6$. Hence $R^2=6.4/10=0.64$, equal to $\rho_{xy}^2=(8/\sqrt{10\cdot10})^2
=0.8^2=0.64$ as @cor-rsquared-range requires.

**Variance estimates.** With $n-p=3$,
$$
s^2=\frac{\mathrm{RSS}}{n-p}=\frac{3.6}{3}=1.2,\qquad s=\sqrt{1.2}\approx1.0954,
$$
and the estimated covariance of $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ is
$$
\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=s^2(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}
=1.2\begin{pmatrix}1.1&-0.3\\-0.3&0.1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}1.32&-0.36\\-0.36&0.12\end{pmatrix}.
$$
Thus the standard errors are $\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_0)=\sqrt{1.32}\approx1.1489$ and
$\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)=\sqrt{0.12}\approx0.3464$.

**The t tests.** By @thm-ttest, under $H_0:\beta_1=0$,
$$
T_1=\frac{\hat\beta_1}{\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_1)}=\frac{0.8}{0.3464}\approx2.309\sim t_3 .
$$
The two-sided $p$-value is $2P(t_3>2.309)\approx0.104$, and the critical value is
$t_{3,0.975}\approx3.182$, so at level $0.05$ the slope is not significant. A $95\%$ confidence interval
for $\beta_1$ is $0.8\pm3.182\cdot0.3464=0.8\pm1.102=[-0.302,\,1.902]$. For the intercept,
$T_0=0.6/1.1489\approx0.522$, $p\approx0.638$. In clinical terms, with only five patients the data are
consistent with no association between baseline severity and outcome change: the confidence interval for
the slope includes zero, even though the point estimate is positive. The study is simply too small to be
conclusive, which is exactly what a nonsignificant $t$ test reports.

**The overall F test.** By the remark following @thm-ftest, testing $H_0:\beta_1=0$ against the full
model,
$$
F=\frac{\mathrm{ESS}_{\mathrm{reg}}/(p-1)}{\mathrm{RSS}/(n-p)}=\frac{6.4/1}{3.6/3}=\frac{6.4}{1.2}
=5.333\sim F_{1,3}.
$$
As promised by the $q=1$ remark, $F=T_1^2$: indeed $2.309^2\approx5.33$. The critical value is
$F_{1,3;0.95}\approx10.13$, so the regression is not significant at the $0.05$ level, consistent with the
$t$ test (the $p$-values agree, both $\approx0.104$).

**Checking the residual maker.** The hat matrix $H=\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top$
has $\mathrm{tr}(H)=2=p$, and $M=I_5-H$ has $\mathrm{tr}(M)=3=n-p$. Numerically the eigenvalues of $M$
are $\{0,0,1,1,1\}$, exactly two zeros (the dimension of $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$) and three ones (the
dimension of $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})^\perp$), illustrating the spectral structure used in
@thm-rss-chisq: $\mathrm{RSS}/\sigma^2$ is a sum of three independent squared standard normals when G3
holds. This is why the divisor is $n-p=3$ and the reference distribution has $3$ degrees of freedom.

**Tying it back.** The same arithmetic, with the treatment-and-baseline design of @exm-lr-running in place
of a single severity column, is what an analyst runs on individual patient data before transporting the
fit to another population. The regression-based population-adjustment methods (simulated treatment
comparison in Part IV, multilevel network meta-regression in Part V) rest on exactly this pipeline: fit a regression, read its coefficients and their uncertainty, and evaluate the fitted model at
a new covariate distribution.

## Notes and references {#sec-lr-notes}

The linear model and its least-squares theory are classical; the treatment here follows the
matrix-geometric viewpoint of @strang2016 for the projection and rank arguments and
@bingham2010regression for the distributional theory (the $t$, $\chi^2$, and $F$ results and the
Gauss-Markov theorem). The two derivations of the normal equations, by calculus and by orthogonal
projection, are the two faces of least squares emphasized throughout @strang2016. The proof that the
scaled residual sum of squares is chi-squared via the spectral decomposition of the idempotent residual
maker, and the proof of the independence of $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ and $s^2$ via uncorrelatedness of
jointly Gaussian blocks, are standard and are given in full in @bingham2010regression; we have supplied
complete proofs of the supporting multivariate-normal lemmas (@lem-mvn-affine-closure,
@lem-gaussian-block-independence) using the moment generating function established in Chapter 4. The
identification of least squares with maximum likelihood under normal errors (@thm-ols-mle-normal) is the
classical justification of the squared-error criterion and is discussed in @bingham2010regression; the
Cramér-Rao efficiency statement (@cor-ols-efficient-normal) connects this chapter to the inference
theory of Chapter 5 (@thm-cramer-rao, @def-fisher-information).

These results recur throughout the book. Simulated treatment comparison (Part IV) fits a linear or
generalized-linear outcome regression on individual patient data and evaluates it at an aggregate
comparator population; multilevel network meta-regression (Part V) writes each arm's linear predictor as
a regression and is, on the identity link, exactly the model of this chapter. The conditional reading of
the coefficients (the remark in @sec-lr-model) is benign here but becomes the subtle issue of
@def-non-collapsibility once a nonlinear @def-link-function is introduced in Chapter 7. The robust
sandwich variance (@def-sandwich-variance) is the standard repair when homoskedasticity (G2) fails.

This chapter has no counterpart in the `ITC_Coq` formalization, whose `OutcomeRegression.v` formalizes
the causal outcome-regression estimator rather than the linear-algebraic least-squares theory developed
here; the results above are pen-and-paper proofs.

## Exercises {#sec-lr-exercises}

A starred exercise, marked $\star$, has a full worked solution in Appendix F. The first three are
accessible warm-ups and interpretation questions; the computation and proof exercises follow.

### Warm-ups and interpretation

::: {#exr-lr-warmup-design}
**(Warm-up) Building a design matrix.** A four-patient trial randomizes patients $1,2$ to control and
$3,4$ to active treatment, with baseline ages $50,60,55,65$. Write the design matrix $\mathbf{X}$ for the
model $\mathbb{E}[y_i]=\beta_0+\beta_1 T_i+\beta_2\,\mathrm{age}_i$, and say which column goes with which
coefficient. Which single entry of $\mathbf{X}$ would change if patient $3$ were instead on the control
arm?
:::

::: {#exr-lr-interpret-coef}
**(Interpretation) Reading coefficients.** In the running example @exm-lr-betahat the fit is
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(1,-1,1)^\top$ for (intercept, treatment, centered baseline severity). State in
one plain sentence each what $\hat\beta_0$, $\hat\beta_1$, and $\hat\beta_2$ mean clinically. If a larger
outcome is worse, is the treatment helping or harming? Which coefficient is the treatment effect that an
indirect comparison would carry forward to another population?
:::

::: {#exr-lr-warmup-compute}
**(Warm-up) A two-point fit.** For $n=2$ with $\mathbf{x}=(0,2)^\top$, $\mathbf{y}=(1,5)^\top$ and an
intercept ($p=2$), compute $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ by hand, the fitted values, and the residuals.
Confirm the line passes through both points, and explain why $\mathrm{RSS}=0$ and why $s^2$ is undefined
here. (Hint: $n-p=0$, so there is no residual degree of freedom.)
:::

### Computation and proof

::: {#exr-lr-simple-formulas}
**Simple linear regression formulas.** For $\mathbf{X}=[\mathbf{1}_n\ \mathbf{x}]$ with $p=2$, solve the
normal equations by hand to show $\hat\beta_1=S_{xy}/S_{xx}$ and $\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x$,
and derive $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta_1)=\sigma^2/S_{xx}$ and
$\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta_0)=\sigma^2\big(\tfrac1n+\tfrac{\bar x^2}{S_{xx}}\big)$ from @eq-cov-betahat.
Verify all four against the worked example of @sec-lr-example.
:::

::: {#exr-lr-centering}
**Centering and the intercept.** Let $\mathbf{X}=[\mathbf{1}_n\ \mathbf{Z}]$ where $\mathbf{Z}$ has
columns with arbitrary means. Show that the slope estimates are unchanged if each column of $\mathbf{Z}$
is centered to mean zero, and that after centering $\hat\beta_0=\bar y$. Interpret this through the
orthogonality of $\mathbf{1}_n$ to the centered columns.
:::

::: {#exr-lr-leverage}
**Leverage.** The diagonal entries $h_{ii}=H_{ii}$ of the hat matrix are the **leverages**. Prove
$0\le h_{ii}\le 1$ for each $i$ and $\sum_i h_{ii}=p$. (Hint: $h_{ii}=\mathbf{e}_i^\top H\mathbf{e}_i$ and
$H$ is a projection, so $h_{ii}=\|H\mathbf{e}_i\|_2^2$; relate this to $\mathbf{e}_i^\top H\mathbf{e}_i$
using $H^2=H$.)
:::

::: {#exr-lr-anova-noint}
**Sums of squares without an intercept.** Show by counterexample that the ANOVA identity @eq-anova can
fail when $\mathbf{1}_n\notin\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$, and identify exactly which step of the proof of
@prp-anova-decomposition breaks.
:::

::: {#exr-lr-gm-weighted}
**($\star$) Weighted least squares and generalized Gauss-Markov.** Replace G2 by
$\mathrm{Cov}(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon})=\sigma^2 V$ for a known positive definite $V$. Define the
weighted estimator $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_V=(\mathbf{X}^\top V^{-1}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top
V^{-1}\mathbf{y}$. Prove it is unbiased with covariance $\sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^\top V^{-1}\mathbf{X})^{-1}$,
and that it is the best linear unbiased estimator under the new assumption, generalizing @thm-ols-blue.
(Hint: factor $V^{-1}=W^\top W$ via the spectral theorem (@thm-spectral-theorem) and transform to
$\tilde{\mathbf{y}}=W\mathbf{y}$, reducing to the ordinary case.) Note the scope: the optimality needs the
weights to be the inverse error covariance. The matching-adjusted estimator of Chapter 18 is also a
weighted estimator, but its weights balance covariates, so this result does not make it optimal.
:::

::: {#exr-lr-general-hypothesis}
**($\star$) The general linear hypothesis equals a nested-model test.** The sampling distribution of the
statistic @eq-glh-stat is established in @thm-general-linear-hypothesis. Complete the picture by showing
that this statistic is identical to the nested-model statistic @eq-fstat, where the reduced model is the
least-squares fit subject to the constraint $R\boldsymbol{\beta}=\mathbf{q}$. (Hint: the constrained fit
minimizes $S(\boldsymbol{\beta})$ over the affine set $\{\boldsymbol{\beta}:R\boldsymbol{\beta}=\mathbf{q}\}$;
solve it with a Lagrange multiplier and compare the two residual sums of squares. The whitening identity
used in the text, that $\mathbf{v}\sim\mathcal{N}_q(\mathbf{0},\sigma^2 A)$ with $A\succ0$ implies
$\mathbf{v}^\top A^{-1}\mathbf{v}/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2_q$, may be quoted.)
:::

::: {#exr-lr-prediction}
**Prediction interval.** For a new unit with regressor row $\mathbf{x}_*^\top$, the point prediction is
$\hat y_*=\mathbf{x}_*^\top\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$. Assuming the new error is independent of the fitting
sample, show that $y_*-\hat y_*\sim\mathcal{N}\big(0,\sigma^2(1+\mathbf{x}_*^\top(\mathbf{X}^\top
\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{x}_*)\big)$ and derive the $1-\alpha$ prediction interval
$\hat y_*\pm t_{n-p,1-\alpha/2}\,s\sqrt{1+\mathbf{x}_*^\top(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{x}_*}$.
Contrast it with the confidence interval for the mean response $\mathbf{x}_*^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}$,
which omits the $1$.
:::

::: {#exr-lr-mle-sigma-bias}
**Bias of the maximum likelihood variance.** Using @thm-ols-mle-normal and @thm-sigma2-unbiased, compute
$\mathbb{E}[\hat\sigma^2_{\mathrm{MLE}}]$ and confirm it equals $\frac{n-p}{n}\sigma^2<\sigma^2$. Explain
why the maximum likelihood estimator is biased while $s^2$ is not, in terms of degrees of freedom.
:::

::: {#exr-lr-rank-example}
**A rank-deficient design.** Let a binary group indicator be coded with both a column of ones and two
group dummies $\mathbf{d}_A,\mathbf{d}_B$ with $\mathbf{d}_A+\mathbf{d}_B=\mathbf{1}_n$, so
$\mathbf{X}=[\mathbf{1}_n\ \mathbf{d}_A\ \mathbf{d}_B]$ has rank $2<3$. Exhibit the one-dimensional null
space $\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{X})$, give two distinct coefficient vectors with identical fitted values, and
identify which contrasts are estimable in the sense of @prp-rank-deficient-pseudoinverse.
:::
